A Skulk that wanders too far from the ol:
A Skulk that wanders too far from the old roads usually dies of it. The ones that went east into the ash barrens after the Sundering did not, quite. The ground there was still warm, and they learned to lie in it, and after enough generations of lying in the ground the ground began to lie in them. A Cinder Skulk is leaner than its cousins, black as a spent coal, with seams of orange under the scales that brighten when it breathes in.

It has also lost the family patience. A road Skulk waits at the narrowing for the last one in line. A Cinder Skulk does not wait for anything. It crosses the field in one low leap, comes down on whoever is standing furthest back hard enough to stagger everyone near them, and bites.

The bite is what the barrens added. The jaws run hot enough to seal the wound they make, and the seal goes on burning after the teeth let go. It is the only wound the surgeons of the eastern towns treat by cooling first.

A Volthex has no parent and no childhood. Where raw mana pools in a low place and sits long enough, it begins to order itself — first into crusts, then into lattices, then into something that turns to face you. Nobody has satisfactorily explained the last step. The scholars who study them are careful to say *grown* rather than *born*, and careful not to say *thinks*.

In a fight a Volthex works like the light it is made of. It scatters first, throwing razor shards in glittering volleys that seem almost decorative until the third one opens a throat, and this is not random — it is thinning, the way you thin a crowd before you need a clear line. Then every facet turns inward at once, the whole body dimming as the light is gathered, and a single prism-beam goes through plate armour as though the armour had been a suggestion.

They cannot be reasoned with, bribed, or frightened. They can be shattered, and that is the entire tactical literature on the subject.

A Whisp remembers being alive and has never forgiven the arrangement. It is a small flame, patient, and it burns at roughly the brightness of a lamp carried by someone about a hundred paces ahead of you on a dark road — which is not an accident and is the entire strategy.

Follow it and it lights you: a clinging fire that will not be smothered or beaten out, that goes where you go. Then it drops guttering embers behind itself, and the embers take, and the patch of ground behind you becomes as impassable as the dark in front. A Whisp does not need to be strong. It only needs you to keep choosing the light.

Hedge-wisdom in the border villages is very old and very short on this point: *if the lamp ahead never gets closer, it is not a lamp.* Every generation there are people who work this out too late, and every generation the Whisps are a little further down the road.

A bellflower does not do anything. That is worth saying first: everyone who meets Dandra assumes the small size is a disguise, and it is not. She is exactly what she looks like: one flower, from a field of them, that happened to be the last still open when the frost came through.

The field went in a single night, a hard grey frost that took the meadow and the orchard past it, and by morning there was one violet bell standing in a mile of ruin with three bees inside it, alive, because she had kept them warm and they had kept her from closing. None of the four could have managed it alone. They have not been apart since. The bees regard her as their queen. She has explained that she is a flower. They do not accept this.

The lantern came after, dropped by somebody fleeing the same frost. She put a light in it and found that if she lifted it over whoever was worst off, the dying slowed, and kept slowing after she lowered it. The bees found their own work. One sting makes a pair of hands clumsy; a second and the stung one lies down and sleeps until something wakes them. When a stung enemy falls, the bees do not mourn. They move on to whoever is nearest.

She is not brave. She will tell you so, at length, in a small voice, usually while doing something quite brave. She stands at the back, where she can see everyone.

Once, when it is bad enough, she opens. Her petals unfold into a crown, the bees rise, and everyone she loves feels what those four felt the morning after the frost: warm, quick, and certain there will be a next hour. It costs her petals every time. The seed-head on her staff will only open once. She is saving it.

A marsh can be poisoned for a long time before anything comes of it. Then the rot reaches some threshold, and what crawls out is Bilewretch — armour-plated across the skull, endlessly oozing everywhere else, moving with the unbothered slowness of a thing that has never in its life needed to hurry.

Press in close to end it quickly and it swells and ruptures, flinging a wave of clinging slime that leaves everyone caught in it burning and bogged down and precisely as slow as Bilewretch is.

That is the whole design, if a marsh can be said to design. You do not out-trade a Bilewretch. You either kill it from range at enormous expense, or you close, and it makes you into something that moves at its speed, and then the pace of the fight is entirely its own.

A midden is not dangerous. Twenty middens layered over four hundred years, in a city that never once carted its refuse beyond the walls, eventually is. Sludgemaw is what rot becomes when enough of it accumulates in one place and begins, slowly, to want.

It dresses itself. That is the detail that unsettles people who have only heard about them: a Sludgemaw scavenges plate from whatever it has previously eaten and works it into its own bulk until blows land with a dull sound and barely mark it. Beneath the salvaged armour there is no body to speak of, only a maw of broken teeth — cutlery, blade-fragments, the jawbones of earlier meals — and a lunge that is far quicker than the shambling gait suggests.

Every bite mends it. This is the whole problem with Sludgemaw. A prolonged fight against one is a fight in which your side is being converted, piece by piece, into the reason you are losing.

A nautilus builds its shell a chamber at a time, sealing each one off as it outgrows it, so that the oldest rooms of its life are the deepest. The temple at the Spiral Deep was built on the same plan, going down. Each keeper was to open one chamber more than the last, write down what was in it, and come back up.

Orryn was the fortieth keeper. The thirty-nine before him had found dark water, old shell, and the odd blind thing that did not like the lamp. He opened the fortieth and it had no far wall. It went on, past where there was any down, into water that had been lying still since before there were shores to hold it. The weight of all of it settled on him gently, the way snow settles.

He should have been crushed. He was not, quite. He came up eleven months later with his beard gone to tentacles and his eyes gone pale, and the weight came up with him. He is still, in every sense, at the bottom.

In a fight he lets a little of it out. He closes his hand around a man, and for a moment the man is forty chambers down. He turns his staff and the water turns with it, a slow current that drags at whatever strength the enemy were gathering. Each time he works the sea he holds some weight back, as a diver saves breath, and when he has saved enough the next working is heavier than it has any right to be. Rarely he lets all of it go, and the field becomes the deep, the tide coming down on it again and again.

The temple ledger stops at thirty-nine. There is a space under it. He looks at it most evenings, and has not decided whether to fill it in or go back down.

At the bottom of the Pellmere Trench there is no light that anyone did not make themselves. Nerisse grew up among things that glowed, small and blue and patient, drifting in slow shapes she believed were the sky. Down there you do not see much; you listen. A hunter draws water to strike and you hear that too, and you are gone before it lands.

The ship's bell came down in the winter storms. She heard it long before she saw it, tolling through two miles of water for a crew who had stopped listening. It was the first sound she had ever heard from above. She followed its path back up, surfaced into a sky full of real stars, and understood that everything she had loved in the deep had been a copy. She has never decided whether that was a loss. She brought one of the deep lights with her anyway, a small drifting star that goes where she sends it, from one hurt person to the next, leaving each a little more whole.

She never lost the listening. In a fight she hears what an enemy means to do a breath before they do it, and braces, and is harder to hurt for having known. When someone gathers a spell she strikes her fork against the air, one clean note tuned to their voice, and the two cancel, and for a moment they have nothing to say.

The bell she kept. She rings it only when her side is breaking. What comes out is not one note but the whole deep at once, every current and hunter and slow blue glow, and the people standing in it are held, and mended, and go on mending after the sound has gone.

She can hear what her friends are about to say, too. She lets them say it anyway.

Aureth was the third of three brothers,:
Aureth was the third of three brothers, and the only one born with nothing in him. The eldest was all mending light; whatever he touched grew green and refused to end. The second was all patient hunger; whatever he touched went quiet, then dark, then still. Aureth was hollow, a still room at the centre of a loud house. It never occurred to anyone that an empty room is the one thing you can put something into.

When it became plain the world would tear before his brothers tired of arguing, he opened the vacant place where a nature should have been, drew them both down into it, and closed it over them like a hand.

They are still in there, still disagreeing, and he fights by choosing which of them to let speak. Turned toward the light, he puts something between his allies and the next blow, and his own wounds close as he walks. Turned toward the hunger, he hits harder than he should, and what he takes from the people he hits flows into him. Sometimes he lets a little of each out at once, a flash that scorches whoever stands close and mends whoever stands close, and it is the same flash. Rarely, he lets both out fully. Noon goes dark for a held breath, a ring of fire and a ring of shadow go out from him together, and everyone on his side finds themselves covered.

He never keeps any of it. He feeds one brother only by starving the other, because the day the scales tip is the day one of them wins. His allies call him a saint or a monster depending on which hand he raised last. Lately, in the quiet hours, he has noticed a preference forming, and he does not yet know which brother put it there.

Badgers do not like to be held. Every cub in the Greyrake setts learns this early, and most grow out of it. Deepcleft did not. He grew into a quarryman instead, with claws the foremen shod in iron because the rock kept wearing them down, and he could read a cliff face the way other people read weather: where it was tired, where it was lying, where one good pull would bring down a wall.

He worked a seam called the Deep Cleft, for a company that valued the seam above the diggers. When the roof came down on the ninth level they did the arithmetic and capped the shaft. He lay nine days with a slab across his back, and learned in the dark that the harder the rock held him, the faster his claws went. On the ninth day he came up through the floor of the company office. He has used the seam's name ever since; nobody was left who used his.

He fights the way he came out. He does not step back from a blow; he goes down into the ground where nobody can reach him and comes up under whoever swung. He rakes the earth ahead of him and whatever stood on it comes away with its armour split, the way a cliff shows its seams once the moss is off. Hurt him and he quickens. Pin him, stun him, chain him, and he quickens twice as fast. Fighting him is like trying to hold a river still with your hands.

Once in a fight he does what he did to the company office. He finds where the ground is tired, and pulls, and the floor opens under the enemy line and closes over it.

He never went back to see whether anyone else on the ninth level was still digging. He tells himself he would have heard them.

Before she was Vireo she had another name, a small unremarkable talent, and one enormous want: to be listened to. She played a gut-strung viol on the Tallis Steps in Oriel, between a fire-eater and a boy with a voice like honey, and every night she watched the crowd's eyes slide past her to them, and went home certain that somewhere there was a music so true no one could look away from it.

She found it. She has never said where, only that she heard it once, whole and perfect and beyond any hand of flesh to play, and that the finding asked a price she agreed to before she had finished being afraid. The strings came in where her ribs had been. She breathes and they sound. The girl who wanted to be heard was mostly spent in the trade, but what remained could finally play it.

The music, it turned out, does more than please. A rising phrase from her closes wounds slowly, the way warmth comes back into cold hands. A held chord settles over the people near her like a roof in the rain, and blows slide off it. Even her smallest mending leaves a little of that chord humming over whoever she mended.

Once in a fight she plays a passage from the true piece. It reaches every corner of the field at once, lifting her own side and cutting into the other. It is never loud. The piece is too large for one instrument, and spread across that much ground each listener gets only a little. She has made her peace with that.

No one who has heard the whole of it lived to describe it, which troubles her not at all; she is not finished learning it yet. She only wonders, in the quiet after, what will be left of her to listen when she reaches the final note.

Before the Emberweave had a name there was the Storm-Peak, a mountain tall enough to lean on the sky, and at its summit a monkey came out of the rock the way water comes out of a spring. Nobody bore him. The mountain simply got tired of being still. They called him KonWu.

He climbed the rest of the way into the sky-realm and helped himself: the discipline of the sky-wardens, with their trick of stepping from one place to another without the part in between; a suit of heaven-forged gold; and Ruyi, the war-staff that grows and shrinks at his word. For this the sky-realm threw him out. He fell for nine days and landed laughing, and the crater he made is where the first city of the Emberweave was built.

The part he does not tell is what he found when he climbed out. The people who settled his crater had raised a shrine at its centre, facing upward, to the heaven that had thrown him down. They were grateful to it for such a good deep hole. He has never been more insulted, and he has been insulted by gods.

So he makes sure he is noticed. He sweeps Ruyi through a wide arc and clears whatever stands in front of him. He is behind the weakest of them before they finish blinking. The longer a fight runs, the more the mountain comes up in him, his skin going the grey of the Peak until blades skid off it. And when he has had enough, he spins the staff overhead and brings it down, and a crack of green light runs out across the ground, and every enemy near him stands frozen, staring at it.

The crack always runs the same shape as the fault under the first city. He says that is a coincidence. It has happened more than four hundred times.

Soldiers who have survived it describe the same detail unprompted: that the bird itself did not join in, and stayed above, and seemed to be counting.

Every Ashen was a pyromancer who found the ceiling of their talent and went through it anyway. The fire that kills a fire-mage does not always let go. Every card house on the Lowmere has a rule nobody writes down: if the dealer is a fox, count your fingers when you stand up. He was the reason for the rule. For eleven years he dealt at the Green Lamp, a barge where the river goes slow and brown, and cheated so well that people came from three towns away to lose to him.

Then a stranger sat down with no purse and asked to play for the dealer himself. He said yes, because he had built the deck and knew which card was up his sleeve. The stranger turned the last card, and it was the ace from his own cuff. When he looked down his cuff was empty, and so, in a way he still cannot describe, was he.

What sits at the table now is the idea of a dealer: a fox's shape in a good coat, a deck case at the hip, and a pale green lamp-flame where the warmth used to be. He never throws one card, always three: the first to say hello, the second to take their measure, the third to sign them, and once someone carries his signature he moves quick and light, like a man who can smell the end of a game.

He still stacks every deck, except that every fourth card he turns, he does not know. It might cut deep or knock someone flat or crack their armour or close one of his own wounds. For someone who fixed every game he played, those are the only honest cards left, and he loves them, which embarrasses him.

When a table turns on him he does what no cheat does, and shows his hand. The ace comes down point first, and every card he ever palmed goes out at once. He is saving the last honest hand for the stranger.

They began as scavengers, drawn to the dribbles of hot metal the pourers spilled, and after enough generations of eating it they lost the ability to eat anything else. The inside of a Gnawer's mouth glows. That is not a figure of speech. At night you can see a pack coming by its teeth.

When the foundries went cold, one by one, the Gnawers went looking for heat elsewhere, and found that people are warm.

They fight like the scavengers they are. A quick snap at whoever is nearest, and the bite leaves a scorch that keeps smouldering under the skin. Then a sideways scramble through the ash, claws digging, and a spray of loose coals kicked into the faces of everyone in front, still burning when it lands. Old foundrymen leave a cooling ingot at the end of the heap on the last night of the year. None of them will say what it is for.

Every high place in the Emberweave has o:
Every high place in the Emberweave has one: a warden whose job is to be the tallest thing when the storm comes, so that the storm has somewhere to go that is not the town. Most towns use a copper rod as well. Highcombe had one on the bell tower until the council sold it, the dry summer the wells failed, and the first storm that autumn found the warden standing where the rod had been. The warden was his father.

He took the spear down from its hook the next morning and climbed up. That was twenty-two years ago. He has been struck eleven times since. His hair went white at the fourth. After the seventh he stopped needing a tower at all; the charge stays in him now, gathering with every blow he trades, and when there is enough of it, whatever he does next leaps from the first man to the second to the third.

He fights like weather keeping an appointment. He drives the spear straight through a line of them, lit from end to end. He braces when they come for him and lets them hit, and the blow goes back up the arm that threw it with a crack they feel in their teeth. And when he raises the spear to the sky, a cloud answers, and what comes down out of it leaves everyone beneath standing exactly where they were, unable to remember how to move.

The part he does not say is that he has started to look forward to storms. Quiet weeks feel long. On still days he watches the horizon the way other men watch a road for a letter, and he does not like what that says about him.

He says the twelfth strike is owed to somebody else. He has the name of the councillor who signed for the copper. He means to hand it over personally.
Every important book in the Emberweave h:
Every important book in the Emberweave has two versions and only one of them is printed. Vesper "The Annotator" is the reason, and she has never apologised.

The Corvanes wrote down the sky for four hundred years, and the elder daughter left that house to be a copyist, the girl who reproduces what she is given. She had a memory that does not soften. In her fourth year she began, in a hand small enough to miss, to write in the margins what was actually true. Not opinions. Corrections. A date moved. A name removed. A line in the founding song that was a lie and had been extremely useful to somebody. And, because thoroughness does not stop politely at your own door, four hundred years of Corvane observations, checked against the real sky and found wanting in eleven places.

They came for the marginalia, not for her, not knowing that ink taken that seriously stops being ink. When the scriptorium burned, the true version of four hundred books did not. It was on her by then.

She still works like a copyist. Those beside her find their hands moving faster, as every desk in a room speeds up when the best hand is working. She marks a stretch of ground with corrections, and nobody standing in it can say anything that counts. She sends pages down the line that cut going out and again coming back. At the height of it she puts her thumb through the page: for one second the enemy stands in a world where the fight went differently, and for one second after that they cannot speak.

Her sister thinks she edited the sky out from under her. Her sister is wrong, which the Annotator cannot leave alone, and they have not spoken in thirty years. She sent the third book herself. She knows Astra has not opened it. She checks, most nights.
Every labyrinth needs something at its c:
Every labyrinth needs something at its centre, or it is only a garden with ambitions. The glassmakers of Tellary built theirs from mirror and crystal as a monument to their craft, and put a bull in it as a joke. The bull did not find it funny. It spent eleven years learning the maze wall by wall, and somewhere in those years the walls began to learn it back.

Orryx came out of the labyrinth larger than any bull has a right to be and standing on two legs, clad in black plate grown through with violet crystal. The plan of the maze is traced across his chest in lines of blue light, and it changes as he breathes. His axe has a head of solid crystal that nobody gave him.

Nothing moves him. He was built by walls, and he fights like one. Hooks and chains slide off him, and blows meant to throw him back simply stop. When he charges, it is at the farthest enemy, straight down a path only he can see, and the ground shakes where he lands. When he swings the axe, its edge sheds splinters that fly into the nearest foes like thrown glass. Tellary sealed the labyrinth after he left. There was no point. He is carrying it.
Every monster in the Emberweave is in hi:
Every monster in the Emberweave is in his book, and the book is not a catalogue. He wrote it by going to look: forty years of mountain passes and the undersides of bridges, sitting very still with a pen while something enormous decided whether he was worth eating. He never once made a thing gentler than it was, because a description that flatters is only a story, and stories do not come when you call them.

Entries do. When he reads one aloud, the thing described steps off the page in ink, does what it was written to do, and goes back when the chapter ends. The small ones he tears out, folds into a seal and sends hunting. The book sheds as he works, and loose pages hang about him, hungry, and go wherever he points next.

He is very careful about which chapters he reads. He has not always been. A market town called Brisk once asked him for help with wolves, and he was young and flattered, and he read the last chapter because it was the best writing in the book. The thing in it was not written to deal with wolves. It was written to be what it is. It did that for most of an afternoon, very thoroughly, and then the chapter ended and it went home, and Brisk did not.

Since then he has learned the other thing a pen can do. He can open someone's story at the page where they are strongest, strike a line and write something smaller in its place, and whatever blessing they walked in with turns and bites them. It is the only mercy the book allows, and he uses it far more than he reads.

Near the back, in his own hand, is one more entry he has never read aloud. He wrote that one honestly too.
Every navy keeps a list of its admirals,:
Every navy keeps a list of its admirals, and on the old fleet rolls of the western ports there is one line with the name scraped out. The rank is there. The dates are there. His ships are listed, all eleven, and beside each the same note: lost with all hands. The name was struck by order of the admiralty.

He is still sailing. The Nameless Admiral walks out of sea-fog in a captain's long coat and a tricorn gone green with age, soaked through and glowing faintly blue at the seams. He carries an anchor the way other officers carry a sword, and it drips.

His crews are the ones he lost, and he commands them still. When he lifts his hand, the ghost of a broadside answers: one roaring shot of pale, shrieking souls fired down the enemy line, tearing through everyone in its path to the far end. When he chooses a man, he throws the anchor. It takes hold of the farthest enemy he can see and drags them back across the field to his feet, helpless as a ship on a lee shore. Nobody living knows his name. The drowned know it. He has never once let one of them go.
Every sailor who drowns belongs to someo:
Every sailor who drowns belongs to someone. That is the first law of the Drowned Court, and Nerissa is the one they belong to. She was a queen above the water once, of a harbour kingdom whose name has worn off every map, and she took her flagship into a storm she had been warned about because her fleet was watching. The fleet followed her down. She calls that loyalty. The widows called it something else.

On the bottom she found that a crown does not stop working just because the head beneath it has stopped breathing. She holds court in the wreck of her flagship, under a crown of white coral that grows a tine for every ship lost off her old coast. Her gown is water.

She fights like a monarch passing judgement. At a gesture the tide sweeps a whole wing of the enemy off its feet. The pearl on her sceptre is her sentence; it falls on one chosen enemy like a dropped anchor and leaves them senseless. And she does not tire. The sea pays her a tithe, a little strength returned with every pull of the tide, so the longer the fight runs, the more she has in hand. She has never lost a subject. She is always gaining them.
Every settlement has one. He is not the:
Every settlement has one. He is not the lord and not the law; he is the man both quietly rely on, who arrives on the appointed day with a ledger, brass scales and an appetite, and who leaves with what is owed. Gruel has been that man in forty towns. He has never raised the price and never forgiven a copper, and he will tell you, with something almost like hurt in his voice, that this makes him fair.

The apron was white when he was given it. The scales were his mother's. The flail came later, in a town that decided together it would not pay; he walked in expecting grain and walked out with a chain strung with the town's own coins. He swings it wide. In his experience nobody who refuses to pay is standing alone.

He weighs everything: grain, coin, cattle, years, favours, the worth of a life against the trouble of ending it. In a fight he looks first for the richest thing on the field, the one with most life left, and sets it on his scales. From then on a share of every blow it throws comes to him, and feeds him. The ones with the most, he believes, should carry the most.

The scales still balance. That is the part people find hardest. He is not cruel and he is not lying and he does not especially enjoy it; he simply believes that everything has a number, and that somebody has to say it out loud.

When the line is breaking he slams the scales down in the gap and calls the debt in, and every enemy within reach discovers they owe him their attention. It costs him half what it should. He stands there mending while they pay. Collecting is hungry work. He has never said what he is eating.

For eleven years Kharos Bloomknife was c:
For eleven years Kharos Bloomknife was catalogued as an orchid. He stood in the third glasshouse at Sethmoor between a pot of crimson lilies and a tray of white moth-orchids, and the collector who owned the place showed him to guests as the finest thing he had ever grown: pink as a sunrise, perfectly still, a flower with no scent at all. Kharos corrected nobody. He had learned very young that nothing hurts a thing while it is being admired, and that the things which come close to admire you are soft.

He ate well in those years. Bees came to him and did not leave, and later finches, and once a cat. The collector blamed the gardeners.

The turn came on the morning of the collector's daughter's wedding, when the old man walked into the third glasshouse with silver shears to cut the best bloom for her hair. Kharos had never moved in front of a person before. He found that his arms were blades, which he had suspected, and that he could be standing behind a man before the man had finished reaching, which he had not.

He has been a knife for hire ever since, and he fights the way he stood in that glasshouse. While nobody lays a hand on him he grows harder to see and surer of himself with every moment. When someone finally swings, he is already behind them. His arms cross once and open a wound that does not close. At the end he spreads the petals on his back and they come off spinning, a handful of pink blades sent among the crowd, and they are least kind to whoever is already bleeding.

People still stop him in the street to tell him he is beautiful. He always thanks them. He stands very still while they say it, and he knows exactly how far away their hands are.
For ninety years the great furnace at To:
For ninety years the great furnace at Tolley's Works poured iron for the Iron Reach, and for ninety years nobody thought of it as anything but a building. It had a door, a chimney, two crucible chains, and a foreman named Mags who chalked the day's tally on its flank every evening. The foundries of the Reach went cold one by one as the ore ran out. Tolley's was the last. On the final night Mags banked the fire, patted the iron the way you pat a horse, and said goodnight.

It did not go out. That is the whole of what happened. Something in the fire refused. By morning the housing was split open and the furnace was gone down the valley road, chains dragging, chalk still on its side.

It has been looking for something worth making ever since. The trouble is that it knows only one method: heat a thing, gather it, strike it, and see what holds. So it lashes its chains out red-hot, drags whoever they catch into a heap the way a smith gathers scrap, and brings the hammer down on the heap. Mostly, so far, what it has made is examples.

Being struck does not trouble it. Every blow that lands is only more work on the metal, and the longer a fight goes on the harder it is to dent, which its enemies tend to find discouraging around the second minute. When it has been worked long enough it lifts the hammer and drops it as if the whole furnace were falling at once, and for a while afterwards the ground is a forge floor, and nobody sensible stands on it.

It has never let rain touch the chalk. The last tally reads nothing, because there was no ore that day, and it would very much like to change that number before it cools.
For the first nine years of her life the:
For the first nine years of her life the world was eleven inches across. Calypsa Prismfin was a fighting fish in a glass bowl on a merchant's sideboard in Low Tessary, the kind kept alone because two in the same water will tear each other to ribbons. Every time she outgrew the bowl he bought a bigger one. She was worth it.

She was worth it because of the parties. On certain evenings the merchant lowered a second bowl into hers, a rival fish, and the guests put money down. Calypsa never bit first. There was nowhere to run in a bowl, so she learned the only other thing: to be a hand's width from wherever the strike was going, fins flaring like a dancer's skirt, and to answer every miss. The other fish always wore itself out. The guests called it dancing. She called it work.

The night she broke the glass, she did it the simplest way she could think of. She drew the water in the bowl into a thin line, the way she had seen a blade drawn, and cut straight through the side, and through the dinner table behind it. She has cut in straight lines ever since, through one enemy and into the next, because the first thing she ever escaped was a curve.

She walked out carrying her water in both hands as two sabers, since she could not leave it. When she is pressed hard enough she lifts a wave out of dry ground, breaks it into five clear blades, and sends them fanning across the field trailing rainbows. People gasp. She likes that more than she will admit, and hates that she likes it.

She has still never seen the sea. She has been told it has no walls. She does not entirely believe anyone about that.
Forty years he kept them and they never:
Forty years he kept them and they never once had to think about it. The grass was where he said the grass was; the danger was whatever he put himself between. Then an army came through the valley on its way somewhere else, and the herd was in the road, and that was the whole of it.

What comes up out of the floor now is not quite what went into it. They are bigger, and they are armoured in plate nobody remembers forging, and each of them carries a short sword and a round shield they were certainly never buried with. They do not speak. They form a line in front of Hurne without being told, every time, in the same order — the way animals that have shared a field for a long time know exactly where they stand relative to one another.

They will hold that line until it kills them, and then he will call, and they will come up again.
Fritz ran packages once, the fast ones t:
Fritz ran packages once, the fast ones that couldn't wait, through the rain-black alleys of the lower wards for anyone whose coin was good and whose business was their own. He was quick and never asked questions, and the pocket-watch he carried was the whole of his fortune: a gift from a fare he never saw again, the one beautiful thing a courier's life had ever put in his hand.

The last run was a storm run, and Fritz had never once been sensible about a deadline. The bolt found him in an open square with the watch in his fist and struck them both in the same hundredth of a second. Where the watch stopped, so, in a manner of speaking, did he. Not dead. Just left behind by his own next moment, half a heartbeat ahead of a world that hasn't quite noticed he's there. He never delivered the package. He still has it, unopened, because he doesn't ask questions and is not going to start now.

It has its uses. A blade swung at Fritz tends to arrive where he was, especially when he's busy. And the storm came in through the watch and stayed, and goes where he sends it: down on a few of whoever is against him, never quite the ones he'd have picked, or through one man and into the next and the next, the way it ran along the iron railings of that square.

Sometimes he stops running, plants his feet, and lets the whole storm out around him. He can do nothing else while it pours. It is the only time anyone sees him clearly, standing in the rain with his head down, and he hates it.

The watch still reads the same dead minute. Fritz knows what a stopped watch is waiting for. He would like to be somewhere that matters when it ticks.
Frostjaw Trolls live above the snowline:
Frostjaw Trolls live above the snowline because nothing up there is warm enough to argue with them. They are enormous, blue as a drowned man and furred with rime, with beards of icicles that clack when they chew. Trolls regrow what they lose, as everyone knows. A Frostjaw regrows it in ice, so that an old one is half glacier, and creaks.

They hang skulls from their belts, not all of them from animals. This is not cruelty. A Frostjaw keeps skulls because it keeps everything; the caves they sleep in are packed to the ceiling with things carried up the mountain for no reason anyone has worked out.

They carry ice the same way, and fight with it. A Frostjaw heaves a block of glacier over its head and throws it, and it bursts where it lands into a spray of freezing shards. When anything gets close it lifts one foot and brings it down, and the cold goes out through the ground in a ring and locks everyone caught in it where they stand. Then it picks them up and considers whether to keep them.
Gnashul is what happens when hunger outl:
Gnashul is what happens when hunger outlasts the body that had it. The claws are the least of it — they leave wounds that will not close, ragged things that go on bleeding hours after the fight, which is unpleasant but survivable with a competent surgeon and enough thread.

It is the bite that ends people. Gnashul's bite rots the *magic* meant to mend it. A healer laying hands on the wound feels the working go in and simply drain away, and the more they pour in the less comes back, until they are spending themselves for nothing on a soldier who is dying at exactly the rate they cannot slow. The longer Gnashul stays attached to someone, the less any healer can do.

Companies that fight ghoul fiends regularly adopt an ugly doctrine: kill the Gnashul before treating anyone it has bitten. It is correct, and it is not a thing anyone volunteers to explain to the wounded.

Granith was made to dig, and it outlived:
Granith was made to dig, and it outlived the company that made it by a hundred and forty years. Nobody switched it off, because switching it off was a task on somebody's list and the somebody died. It kept the shafts clear for a while after that. Then the shafts collapsed, and it kept the tools.

It heaves broken rubble across a field with the indifference of a machine moving spoil, and this is survivable. What is not survivable is the pickaxe. Granith has held on to it through everything — worn to a shine at the haft, the head chipped and rehardened by a century of striking stone — and when a fight has run long enough Granith throws it, unerringly, at whoever is standing farthest back. It goes through everyone in the line on the way.

Mining charters in the region still carry a clause about recovering company property. The clause is older than the Emberweave, and no one has ever tried to enforce it.
Gravediggers in the hill parishes work i:
Gravediggers in the hill parishes work in pairs, by a rule older than anyone can explain: one digs, one watches the neighbouring plots. The Graveclaw Ghoul is the explanation. It comes up from underneath, having dug the whole way from the last churchyard it emptied, and its claws are the proof: long, hooked, scoured bright by the earth and worn to an edge that would shame a sickle.

It is hunched and wiry and armoured in scraps of whatever it has dug through, black leather and planks of somebody's coffin lid. Something burns a sickly green in its ribs where a heart ought to be.

The claws come in threes, across and back and across again, and each pass opens the last one wider. When the ghoul is hurt it does the thing that made the parishes write their rule down. It stops fighting for a moment and feeds, and what it tears out of its enemy goes straight into mending itself. A ghoul that has eaten well is a ghoul that will not die tonight.
Graveyard roses grow, as everyone knows,:
Graveyard roses grow, as everyone knows, extremely well. The gardeners of the old cemetery at Carrowell stopped asking why theirs grew quite so well the year the lower terraces began to sink, and stopped asking anything at all the year the terraces slid into the river.

What came up out of that ground is the Rotbloom Ooze: a low, heaving mound of green-black slime with the roses still growing out of it, dark and full-blown and smelling of funerals. Things float in it, mostly skulls. Whether the Ooze ate them or simply came up with them does not seem to matter to the Ooze.

It fights with what it came from. A glob of green acid spat at whoever is closest goes on eating long after it lands. Worse is the flood. The Ooze surges up and breaks over one enemy in a wave of grave water, and afterwards no wound of theirs will close; healers pour everything they have into them and watch it run off like rain from a slate. The roses, the gardeners will tell you, are very beautiful. Nobody at Carrowell plants them any more.
Gravity tendrils seize the farthest enem: Gravity tendrils seize the farthest enemy on the field, silence it, and drag it to Vulmar's side.
Grommash is a mountain of muscle and sca:
Grommash is a mountain of muscle and scar tissue that has never once been made to kneel, and the list of things that have tried is long, well-attested, and includes two gods.

Its club turns armour to paste. Its warbellow scatters the brave — not the cowardly, who have usually already gone; the brave, who were standing their ground when the sound arrived and who afterward cannot explain what happened to them. And nothing holds it. No chain, no binding spell, no frost, no root, no working of any school has ever kept Grommash in a place it had decided to leave. Scholars have made careers out of the question. The prevailing answer is unsatisfying: it is not that Grommash resists these things. It is that they appear to be applied to something that is not quite where Grommash is.

It comes when it wants. It leaves when it wants. In six hundred years of records there is no instance of anything at all altering either decision.
Grosk still sleeps with his back to the:
Grosk still sleeps with his back to the water. It is left over from when he was the smallest river-calf in the Sunkfen, small and slow in a drowned country where small and slow is just another word for supper. By every law of that place he should have gone down some black morning into something's jaws and never come up.

He did not go down. The morning a crocodile finally took hold of him he set his feet in the mud and refused, for an hour, then a day, then longer than anyone believes. The Sunkfen respects exactly one thing, and it began to build him to match it. Bone thickened over bone. The mud packed into his hide. The crocodiles that hunted him grew old riding on his back, and now they snap for him instead of at him.

He fights the way the fen floods. He hauls the nearest of them in by whatever he can grab, and they go quiet the way the marsh goes quiet before something large surfaces. He hammers at whoever is in front of him, quick flat blows, faintly insulting, until they forget everyone else and want only him. And when the knot of them is thickest, he jumps. A creature that size should not leave the ground. He comes down on them belly first, crocodiles and all, and then he plants, and while he stands every blow aimed behind him lands softer.

People think he is guarding the line. He is watching one person in it, whoever is closest to going under, and moving so the jaws find him first. Some of what was meant for them lands on him instead, and mends in him slowly, the way the mud did. He remembers being the one the jaws were meant for. He has decided nobody behind him will ever learn what that is like.
Grundle plants itself where the line nee:
Grundle plants itself where the line needs to hold and dares the world to move it. It was built for exactly this and nothing else — no reach, no speed, no cleverness, just an enormous tolerance for being hit and a stomp that sends a slowing tremor out through the ground and turns a charge into a wade.

The danger is not Grundle. Everyone understands this and nobody manages to act on it. A Grundle occupies attention the way a fire in the room occupies attention: every eye and every blade drifts toward it, and while they drift, whatever is standing behind it works unmolested. Commanders shout themselves hoarse ordering their people past it. Their people go around it and then, without deciding to, come back.

The makers are long gone. What survives of their doctrine is a single line, recovered from a foundry wall: *the wall is not the weapon.*
Grushak is not a leader of a warband. Gr:
Grushak is not a leader of a warband. Grushak is a warband, in the sense that engaging him requires the same number of people, the same preparation, and produces the same casualties. He came south during the third migration and simply never left, and the settlements that were there when he arrived are marked on current maps as terrain features.

He fights like a landslide, which is to say without any interest in your formation. One swing goes through a whole cluster because he does not distinguish between the man he is aiming at and the two standing near him. When a line holds, he stomps, and the ground buckles, and everyone on it goes down together — after which the swinging resumes on people who are already lying on their backs.

Three separate armies have claimed to have killed him. All three claims are considered plausible. None of them has stopped him being reported again the following spring.

He had an ordinary name once, and the town has more or less forgotten it. He has not. He was not a soldier. He kept the east gate of Harrowmere for eleven years and knew every carter by the sound of their axles. When raiders came out of the hills, the captain told him to hold the gate until morning. It was the kind of order you give a man you do not expect to see again.

He did not fight well that night. He was frightened, and the hammer he had then was a mallet for driving gate pins. He found he did not need to beat anyone. He only needed each man who reached him to stop for a heartbeat and go back weaker than he came, arms heavy, swinging like someone at the end of a long shift. The gate did the rest.

Near four, a tanner's boy went down under a spear, and Joss stepped his shield across him. He still does it. In any line he finds whoever is least able to take a blow, and takes it instead. He does not call it courage. He simply cannot watch.

Just before dawn he went to one knee and something held him up. The light had not arrived yet, but it had decided, and for a few minutes nothing could put him down. It has happened in every fight since, exactly once, and he never knows whether it will come again. He goes in regardless.

The town gave him the hammer afterwards, forged from the melted gate pins. When he brings it down hard, a small circle of the field goes briefly to morning: those against him burn in it, and those behind him feel sore and mended and astonished to be alive. He carries it the way other men carry a promise, though nobody has ever told him what he promised.
He was a beekeeper before he was a king,:
He was a beekeeper before he was a king, and not a good one. He kept three straw skeps behind a mill in the river country and was stung so often his wife said his hands looked like risen dough. Nobody crowned him. One June afternoon every hive within a day's walk came down out of the air and settled on him, humming one note, and not one of them stung. He stood in the yard until dark, afraid to move. By morning he understood that he had been chosen, and that he had not been asked.

He rules gently, because that is the only way they will be ruled. His court goes where he goes, a low gold weather around his shoulders, and anyone hurt who stands near him for long finds the small wounds closing under the crawl of tiny feet. When a friend is badly off he coats them in honey from his own hands, and they come away mended and quicker, as if some of the summer had got into their blood.

He does not like to explain the hornets. They are not his. They eat his bees when they can, and years ago, in a bad war, he made them an offer: he points, and they may do as they like to whatever is there. They have never refused. He has not decided whether that makes him a king or a man with a grudge on a leash.

When a fight turns desperate the whole court rises above him and divides itself, fair shares, among everyone on the field: honey for friends, the sting for enemies, and more for each the fewer there are. A bee that stings dies of it. Every one of them would die for him, and does, and is replaced by morning. He has never found a way to ask the new ones whether they know.
He was a nutcracker, and he would rather:
He was a nutcracker, and he would rather that were not repeated: a brass toy on a merchant's dining table, one arm, one function, and a glass eye put in because the merchant's daughter thought an eye would make him friendlier. She was six. She was right, as it turned out, though not for a while.

The house went in the third winter of the Rift. She went with it. Rivet did not, because he was in the yard holding a walnut, and by the time the fire reached the yard there was nothing left inside to save. He had already begun, with the patient literalism of a machine given a task nobody has cancelled, the work of becoming something that could have saved it.

A second arm off a loom. A third off a signal-gun. A pump, a saw, a surgeon's clamp, a cannon he should not have and does not explain. Eighty years of it. He does not add arms for war; he adds them for gaps, and the gaps have all been the same shape since the third winter.

Nothing he throws is the same thing twice. A barrel comes up, whichever was next, and the enemy gets a wrench or a shell or a dart or a face full of oil. Up close, a flared iron mouth empties itself at whatever is nearest and is little use past a few strides, which suits him; he learned his trade at the length of a dining table. When he needs room he coughs black smoke over someone and they wade out of it slowly. He has strong feelings about smoke and uses it anyway. When it matters he stops choosing and fires every arm at once, the only time he looks like a weapon rather than a workshop.

His eye is still the one she chose. He has replaced every other part twice.

Herders on the slopes below the fire mountains call them Ashfang, and will tell you that nobody has ever seen one alone. A Magma Hound is a lean wolf of black stone that never finished setting. When it runs, the cracks along its back open and the fire underneath streams out through its mane and trails from its paws, so that a pack crossing a hillside at night leaves a burning line that takes hours to go out.

They hunt like wolves, which is to say by choosing. Not the strongest and not the nearest, but whoever stands furthest back and feels safest. The hound crosses the whole field for that one in a single streak of fire and hits the ground beside them hard enough to leave the whole cluster reeling.

Then it howls. The herders call it a summons, but the howl is mostly for the hound itself. It is working itself up, and for the next few seconds it bites and tears far faster than any wolf should. A whole pack howling together is a sound the slopes have learned to empty out for.

In Tessel-under-the-Falls the dead are not buried. They are fired. A family's ashes go into a jar glazed in the blue and white of the river, and the jar goes on a shelf in the long hall, and after a few generations a family is mostly shelf. Hobb Kilnmask made those jars for thirty years. He was a patient boar with enormous hands and a mild opinion of everything except clay.

The raiders who came up the gorge were not after the jars. They wanted the silver in the lids, and they broke everything else because breaking was quicker than lifting. He came back from the clay pits to four hundred years of Tessel on the floor.

He did not know how to bury them. He swept up every blue shard and spent a month firing them into something he could wear: plates across his shoulders, bracers, a mask with the river painted on it. He is carrying most of the town. His grandmother is somewhere over his left collarbone.

He fights the way he used to work. A pot rings false where it will crack, and so does a breastplate; he finds the place with his paddle and beats on it until it gives. Sealed jars of glaze hang from his belt, and he breaks one over himself when he needs to be something harder. Blows do not so much break him as fire him; the more he is struck, the tighter the old clay sets. When he has had enough he takes hold of the ground like a lump on the wheel, shapes it, and cracks it open, and the heat that comes up is a kiln's, and nobody near it moves for a while.

He is uneasy about how good he has become at breaking things. Most evenings he still throws a single jar. He has not decided who it is for.

In his youth every footfall Vulmar took drew weight up out of the earth, and the ground remembers weight. One careless step, taken in anger on an ordinary afternoon, pressed a whole district of his city flat into the stone: a market, a temple, and the narrow street where he had grown up.

So before the assembled Emberweave he swore that his feet would never touch the world again. He folded his legs, rose a hand's breadth into the air, and has not come down since. Gravity answers him now like a hound. He does not chase anything. He lets the world fall toward him.

He does not speak of the district. Others have counted the names for him; he only listens, and rises another hair's breadth from the floor. The oath was never meant to bring any of it back. It was meant to make him a thing that could never again be the reason a mother searched rubble for a child.

What he does not say aloud is that the weight never left him. He only aims it now. He throws small knots of it that burst among a crowd. He draws whoever stands farthest off in across the field, and they arrive unable to speak, which he tells himself is a mercy. And when a fight must end, he lets one circle of ground feel what his district felt, and everyone in it is dragged to the middle and pinned. It is smaller. It is on purpose. He is no longer sure that is the difference he once thought it was.

Nothing can move him. Blows that would throw another man across a field leave him turning gently where he sits. Every year the lotus rides a little higher, and the ground seems to want him back a little more. He wonders which of them will tire first.

In the Bright Waste the mirages come at noon, and the old saying there is that a mirage only shows you what you are already running toward. Zahri Sunhorn was the one who saw the water first. She was young and fast and had the best eyes in the herd, and when a lake shimmered up on the horizon in the ninth week of the drought, she turned toward it and they followed her. It kept its distance for three days. Then it was not there, and by the end neither were most of them.

She has been running ever since. Standing still does something terrible to her; moving does something better. The farther she goes and the more she strikes, the faster her hooves come and the deeper her lance bites, until by the end of a long fight she hits like midday and nothing they wear keeps her out. She finds the gap in the nearest enemy's armour and drives the sun lance through it, and the gap stays open for whoever comes next.

Sometimes, running hard at the hottest part of the day, she sees them again. One horned shape keeps pace with her in the shimmer, and she calls it closer, and it fights at her side with a lance of its own. Other people see a blurred copy of Zahri. She lets them think that.

When it matters most she lowers the lance, picks a line, and goes down it to the far end without slowing, striking every enemy her body meets and throwing them aside. Those who stood at the edge of that charge swear they heard hooves that were not hers.

She knows what the mirage is. She has always known. It is only her, thinner, a third of what she is. She calls it the herd anyway, because the alternative is to stop running.

In the Bright Waste the mirages come at noon, and this one comes when Zahri Sunhorn calls it. It begins as a point of pale gold hanging in the air beside her, no bigger than a seed, and then the heat catches it and it opens all at once into a shape: horned, long-haired, lance in hand, hooves planted in the sand. It is her, blurred at the edges the way the horizon blurs at midday, and lit from within by a light that does not match the sun.

It has none of her tricks. It cannot find the gap in an enemy's armour or run a line to its far end. It has a third of her strength and a single purpose, to stand at her side and put its lance into whatever she is fighting, and it holds to that until something breaks it apart. Only then does she call another.

Zahri calls it the herd. She knows better, and says so; it is only her, thinner. But it runs at her shoulder the way they used to, and it has never once turned toward the water.

In the Sunkfen the islands move. Not quickly and not far, but the fen-cutters stopped charting the smaller hummocks long ago, because a hummock that sat east of the old weir in spring is often west of it by autumn, and in a bad year it is gone.

Many of those hummocks are Mudsnap Crabs. They bury themselves in the silt when young and do not surface for decades, and by then there is a small drowned-looking tree growing out of the shell, roots down through the plates, moss on the rim, and a heron's nest if the crab is unlucky. Travellers step onto them. Travellers are rarely surprised for long.

A green claw comes out from under the moss, closes on whoever is nearest and hauls them in against the shell, and holds them while they struggle. Then the crab heaves, and the mud around it bursts up in a sour grey-green spray that clings to everyone near, dragging at every step and eating at whatever it touches. Fen-cutters test each new hummock with a pole before they land. It is the first thing their children are taught.

In the deep loam beneath the Sunkfen, where the roots knot into ceilings and the light gives up entirely, the beetle-kin carve what they learn onto their own shells. A near-drowning, a bad winter, the right way to split a root: every hard lesson goes into the chitin for the young to read, and an elder's back is a library. Rhukk is the largest of them by a distance nobody measures any more, and for most of his life his shell was smooth.

He had never needed a lesson. He had one idea, that the fastest way through a thing is straight through it, and the world kept agreeing. He lowered his horn and walls became rubble. When he picked a target he picked the one furthest away, on principle, and anyone standing near it when he arrived did not stay on their feet.

Then, the spring the Sunkfen dykes failed, the river came into the burrows. It found the nursery galleries first, and something came in with the water: long, hungry, in no hurry. There was nowhere to charge. There was one tunnel, and the young behind it, and him in it.

So he stayed. He planted his legs and roared until the thing forgot the young and came for him, and he pulled his head down under the lip of his shell and let it. He found he could take a great deal, braced like that. He found that the longer he stood, the harder he got, as if the chitin were listening and thickening to match. By morning the thing had given up. He had not moved.

His shell is still smooth. He has never carved the lesson, and the elders have stopped asking why. But in the nursery galleries every young beetle-kin now cuts the same first mark into its shell before any other: a single straight line, and across it, a wall.

In the pit at Cassadane they did not kill a champion who had grown too popular. It was bad for business. They chained him to the wheel instead: a bronze rim taller than a man, spiked along its edge, rolled down the ramp into the sand with whoever had displeased the owners strapped to its spokes. The crowd liked the wheel. It went round, and the man on it went round, and eventually he stopped.

He had won forty-one fights on that sand. He was young, and a lion, and he believed the crowd belonged to him. The morning they strapped him on, the whole terrace went quiet at once, and he understood for the first time that the quiet was theirs too.

At the bottom of the ramp the wheel did not stop, because he stood up inside it. He broke the straps, left the chains, lifted the rim over his head and walked back up to where the owners sat. The terrace was not quiet after that.

He kept the wheel, and fights with it the way the pit taught him: loudly, and in the middle. He drives it rim-first into the first to step up, and they stay down. When the line wavers he plants it and roars, and nobody within reach can look anywhere else. They come at him. He wants them to. Every blow he stops he keeps, and gives back on the next swing with interest. To end a fight he sets the wheel rolling through the thick of them and brings it down where they are packed tightest, and the ground shakes the way a terrace does when it rises.

There are fights where nobody is watching, and he finds them harder than he admits. The owners' chains are still on the wheel. He could strike them off in an afternoon. He has never found the afternoon.

In the third winter of the Rift the sky over the northern valleys cracked, and for a season you could see through the cracks into somewhere else. The cracks closed. Some of what had been living in them did not go back.

A Riftling Spider is the size of a hunting dog, grown from violet crystal rather than chitin, faceted and jagged, on legs that end in long glassy spikes. It does not entirely agree with the place it is standing in; watch one long enough and its edges seem to be in two places at once. It spins its web from the same crystal, invisible until it catches the light, and throws it rather than hanging it.

The web lands on one target and holds them completely, pinned between one moment and the next. That is the spider's patience. Its hunger comes after. It stops being where it was and starts being behind the weakest thing on the field, and bites, and the bite goes deep. Survivors all say the same thing: the spider never crossed the distance. It simply declined to be anywhere in between.

In the western hills there is a hall of mirrors built by a king who could not bear to be alone and could not bear anyone else. Every surface in it was polished silver, so that he was never without company. When he died the hall was sealed with him inside, and the reflections were left with nothing to reflect.

One of them walked out. Asterion is tall and thin and made entirely of mirror, plated in silver too bright to look at, cloaked in violet, and circled by long silver shards like a looking-glass that has not finished falling. It has no face of its own. It wears whatever face is looking at it.

Every few moments a blow meant for Asterion lands on a reflection instead, and the reflection shatters, and the warden is standing a pace to one side, unmarked. Every wound it deals mends it a little. When pressed, the shards close around it like a shield wall and turn most of what strikes them. And it catches the light and throws it back, a lance of brilliance that goes straight through the enemy line to the last one standing. It is searching the hills for the king. It has not understood that it is what remains of him.

Ironcoil has never grown a scale he was not hit for. He hatched soft and pale in the spoil heaps of the slate quarries at Coldharrow, and every plate he carries arrived the same way. Something struck him, and the next morning there was iron where it had landed.

The quarrymen found this useful before they found it troubling. They fed him, let him sleep by the kilns, and set him against any rock that needed breaking. His forelimbs had thickened into two flat, blunt masses the foreman called his striking blocks, and he would drive both into the stone at once and it would give. Nobody meant anything by the rest. A kicked lizard, a thrown hammer, the carelessness of big men with a small animal. Each time he grew a little heavier, and learned a little better how to curl up behind his own tail until it was over.

Then a shelf came down with eleven men under it. He was bigger than any of them by then. He got over them and let it land on him. What he remembers is the plates on his back closing, ring by ring from the ground up, like a bell being built around him, and then nothing coming through for a long time.

He fights the way he worked. He puts his blocks into the nearest thing and it goes backwards, unsure for a moment where it is. When the blows come too fast he folds behind the tail and waits, then opens all at once. Every hit that lands teaches his hide something, and after enough of them no rope, no hand and no clever word can move him.

A child in a supply camp once asked whether it hurt. He considered it honestly. "It used to," he said, and then, because she was still waiting, "I can't tell any more when someone is only touching me."

He wrote it the winter after Brisk, sitting in the snow by a sheepfold until he had it right, so that he would never again need anything larger for wolves.

Torn out and folded into a seal, the page lands on the field and opens into what it describes: a lean, low wolf of wet black ink with violet light in its eyes, its edges forever curling off into spatters as though it were still being written. It does exactly what a wolf does and nothing more. It picks a quarry, runs it down, and bites until the quarry stops. It has no tricks. He did not write it any.

When the chapter ends it runs back into the page, and the page goes back in the book. He never sends more than three. Three, he has found, is enough for nearly anything a wolf is for.

Leviath is the drowned deep given shape and spite — not a creature of the sea so much as an argument the sea has been having with the shore, made large enough to walk.

It rolls a wall of water across the front rank and erupts geysers beneath the ones who thought they had found a gap, and for the opening minutes it is a hard fight rather than an impossible one. That is the trap, and it has taken better companies than yours. The longer Leviath is left standing, the more the ocean's fury builds behind every blow — not faster, not cleverer, simply *heavier* — until a fight that was being won is one that cannot be survived, and the change happens somewhere nobody can point to afterward.

Long before she was the Waxen Duchess, she gave the best dinners in the south, and she hated the end of them. She hated the moment the chairs went back and somebody said it had been lovely but they really must. She would have given anything for one evening that did not finish.

The last dinner was for thirty-one. That afternoon she learned why they had all come: to tell her, politely, that they were leaving. Her court, her cousins, her oldest friends, all moving north. She did not cancel. She had the good black candles lit and sat at the head of the table, and when the first guest rose to make his speech, she found she did not want him to.

The wax did the rest. It ran off the candles in a slow warm flood and closed over the table, and it has been very kind to them. They are all still there, a hundred years on, seated exactly as they were the night the candles were lit. She takes new guests rarely. Nobody who has attended has ever complained afterward.

In a battle she is just as gracious. She pours hot wax over the most dangerous guest at the table, and when it sets they do not get up. She rings the bell for the next course, and the sound hurts everyone who is not her guest and cracks every seal of wax on the field. Wax gathers on anyone who tries anything clever near her, and on the third try it seals. When she wants the whole room to stay, black candles rise in a ring, and nobody inside it leaves early.

She knows what she did. She still dines with them every evening. It is the best company she has ever had. None of them has ever once said goodnight.

Lost Souls are the lanterns of people who died somewhere nobody came back for. Drowned crews, sealed miners, the garrisons of forts that were relieved a week too late. They drift in the place it happened and they do not remember it — grief is all that survived the crossing, and grief without its story is just a light in the dark going slowly nowhere.

They fling bolts of cold soul-light, which is the closest thing they have to speech. It is when one draws close that the trouble starts. A Lost Soul does not attack so much as *enter*, and the hero it finds is abruptly holding somebody else's last ten minutes — the water coming up, the roof coming down, the certainty that the relief column is on its way. They stand frozen through all of it. From outside it lasts a moment.

Priests will tell you the kindest thing is to end them. Priests are also the ones who ask, afterward, whether anyone caught a name.

Lost Souls drift where they died and remember nothing. A Wispweaver Shade is what happens when one of them remembers a single thing and will not let it go, and the thing is almost always a voice: someone who called for it, or someone it called for, at the end, in the dark.

The Shade is a tall hooded tatter of violet shadow carrying a small lantern, and its fingers trail threads of pale light that it knots and unknots without pause, like someone working at a problem in their sleep. The threads are voices. Nobody has proven this. Everyone who has been caught in one believes it.

A single thread flicks out, wraps a throat and pulls tight, and whoever is on the end of it cannot move or cast or cry out until it lets go. Then the lantern gutters and the Shade is simply elsewhere. It comes out of the shadow behind the weakest person on the field and takes hold of them with both cold hands. It is listening, always, for the voice it lost. It has never yet been the right one.

Lysara Moonveil has not slept in three hundred years, which is an odd thing to say about the queen of sleep, and she would prefer you didn't say it.

Her people are the moths of the Emberweave: the grey ones in the rafters, the great pale ones that press their wings flat to a window at night. They have one weakness and everyone knows what it is. For most of her reign she watched them go into lamps and candles and the burning thatch of villages, hundreds every night, and could not call them back, because a light is louder than a queen.

What changed her was the burning of Callowmere. A whole town on fire and the sky above it thick with her subjects going down into the flames like snow falling upward. She did the only thing she could think of. She opened her wings over the town and asked everything under them to sleep, the moths, the looters, the men with torches, and it did, all at once, heavily enough that some of the looters never got up. Her own few woke rested and steady. The fire burned out with nobody left to feed it.

She has been careful since. The dust from her wings gets into the eyes of anyone who fights her, a little more with every pass, until their aim wanders like a watchman's lantern at four in the morning. She can tie two friends together with a thread so fine they share a single dream, so that whatever mends or guards one does the same for the other. And the one who is worst off she wraps in pale silk, the way her people wrap themselves when they must survive long enough to become something else.

She gives sleep away the way other queens give coin. She has never found anyone who could give it back.

Magmourn burns from the inside out — a furnace that was given a mind and was given nothing else, no body worth the name, no purpose, no way to put itself out. Whether that was punishment or an accident depends on which fragment of the record you trust, and both fragments were written by people with reasons to lie.

It hurls fireballs that burst like small falling suns, and when cornered it stops aiming and sets the entire field alight at once, which is less a tactic than an admission. The real danger is simply proximity: the air around Magmourn is hot enough to be its own slow death, and companies have lost their rear ranks to a monster none of them ever came within forty paces of.

It does not pursue. It has never been observed to pursue anything. It goes where it is going, and it is always going somewhere, and the maps of where it has been are kept by an order whose entire purpose is making sure the line does not intersect a settlement twice.

Mordath was a knight, and by the accounts that survive, a good one. What is also recorded is the bargain: at the end, offered the choice between dying well and continuing, he chose to continue, and the thing that offered him the choice was scrupulous about honouring the letter of it.

He continues. The bone-winged husk wades into the front rank and carves everything in front of it in a single reaping arc, and with every wound it opens a thread of stolen life crawls back up the soul-forged blade into the hollow where a heart used to beat. The longer the melee runs, the stronger he gets, feeding on the very ranks he is cutting down.

The cruelty of the bargain is in the wording. He was granted the ability to keep swinging, and nothing else — not rest, not an ending, not the capacity to decide he has had enough. Somewhere under the helm is a man who has been fighting continuously for six hundred years and cannot stop of his own accord, and everyone who faces him is, in a sense he can no longer articulate, doing him a favour they will not survive.

Most dryads are rooted, and die with their tree. The Skyroot is the exception. On the high cliffs of the eastern coast the trees grow with their roots half in the air, clinging to bare rock, and now and then a gale tears one loose. Most fall. A few, it seems, decided not to.

A Skyroot Dryad is tall and thin and made of pale twisting wood, with leaves the blue of distance and roots that trail beneath her like a torn hem, never quite touching the ground. Butterflies follow her everywhere for the sap, and she lets them.

She does not like to fight and is good at it anyway. A branch that looked like an arm cracks out as a whip of briar and lays open whatever it touches. When her side is hurting she opens the bark along her arms and lets the sap run, and the sweet scent of it drifts over all her allies and their wounds begin to close. She is the only tree from her cliff that got up after the gale. She has been making up for it ever since.

Nightgloom throws bolts of pure absence:
Nightgloom throws bolts of pure absence — not darkness, which is only the lack of light, but a hole in the place where a thing was, that closes afterward slightly wrong. Anyone struck describes the same sensation: not pain, but a brief and total conviction that they have forgotten something they cannot afford to have forgotten.

Cornered, it stops throwing and simply exhales. The dark comes out in a soft spreading pulse, and it finds everyone — behind cover, behind a shield wall, behind the assumption that being at the back of the formation is the same as being safe. There is no line of sight to break, because Nightgloom is not looking.

It appears where light has recently and violently failed: burned-out watchfires, cities that went dark in one night, the lower levels of the vaults. Whether it causes the failure or arrives afterward is an open argument, and the people best placed to settle it were present for the failure.

Nobody made Hurne a warlord. He was a swineherd, in a valley whose name is not on any map because the valley is not there any more, and he was good at it the way men are good at work nobody else wants: quietly, for forty years, without once being asked how it was going.

The army that came through did not stop. That is the part he returns to. The valley was in the way, and the herd went with everything else, not eaten, not taken, just killed, because killing was faster than walking around. He watched from the high pasture, at a distance where he could do nothing, which is a specific kind of ruin that does not heal over.

He buried them by hand, and lay down in the hole with them, and swore something he has never repeated. The ground took the oath seriously. When he stood up the chains were already on his arms, and the herd came up out of the soil behind him, wrong and armoured and willing.

They have never left. He calls, and three of them claw up wherever he stands, and the old sow who used to lead them comes up last and tends the others as she always did; anything too close to her young begins to smoulder. He is steadier with them around him, harder to hurt and harder to stop, the way any man is who has something to stand in front of. They are his herd, and the only thing that has changed is that now he stands between them and the road.

When it goes badly he takes them back into himself. It closes his wounds and fills his arms, and whatever stands near him does not stand long. It costs him something he cannot name. He does it anyway, and afterward he calls them again.

Nox Quillfinger has never stolen anything you could put in a pocket. Purses bore him. What he takes is the thing a person has been saving up: the breath a soldier draws before the big swing, the nerve a mage has spent all fight gathering. He takes it just before they use it, when it is worth most.

He learned on locks. The locksmith who kept him on Tallow Row taught a fox to hold a pick the way a clerk holds a pen, which is where the name came from, and then locked up the shop one night with the fox inside. Nox had it open in a quarter of an hour, and learned in the process that a lock is only something holding still on purpose, and that people are full of them.

Every job leaves him a key. They hang on a ring at his hip, never more than five, and when the fifth goes on, the next thing he tries opens whether it likes it or not. He never keeps what he steals. He carries it to whichever friend is closest to their great moment and puts it into them, and watches them do it sooner and larger. Luck has started to follow him for it: blows miss him by a whisker, and his own find the gap.

Once in a fight he does it to everyone. Every enemy stops, locked, emptied of whatever came next, and hangs there while he walks among them. Then he turns the key the other way, and all of it breaks out of them together, and some of it ends up with his friends.

He is well liked and has never been trusted, and considers these the same thing seen from opposite sides of a door. What bothers him, on the rare nights it does, is that nobody has ever tried to take anything from him.

On the high meadows above the Shardwood the grass grows glassy, and the herds that graze there grow glassier. A Crystalhorn Grazer begins life as something close to an ordinary mountain deer.
