That is a small thing to be. She knows it is a small thing to be. She watched larger powers come through the Emberweave and level cities, and there was a stretch of a few centuries where this bothered her considerably.

What changed her mind was a siege — not the breaking of it, she had nothing to do with that. It was the fourth morning, when the wall was still holding and everyone on it had privately decided it would not hold a fifth, and the light came up the way it does, and three hundred people who had already given up quietly decided to try again. Nobody healed anybody. Nobody was stronger. They simply became willing.

Whatever a person was shouting at three in the morning, they are not shouting it when the light comes — and she found that if she wanted, she could reach into a fight and take one voice out of it, briefly, the way the dawn takes every voice out of a street. Whatever she is now, it kept that. She comes up out of the ground last, always, after the others are already standing, and the first thing she does is walk the line and put the sick ones right. The chant is not a language anyone has identified and the bone-staff was not made by hands; the effect is simply that wounds close near her, and that anyone who crowds her herd begins, without being touched, to burn.

Hurne does not give her orders. It has been observed, more than once, that when the two of them are on a field together it is not entirely clear which one is being followed.

She was eight days old when the mountain opened, and she lived only because her mother was carrying her down the slope to show a cousin. Behind them, the village went under a river of stone in the time it takes to say a name, and the ground there cooled to black glass. The survivors had a word for the thing that did it, a surveyor's word nobody had needed before. Pyroclast. She grew up hearing it said the way other children hear the name of a wolf.

At sixteen she climbed back up alone to have it out with the mountain. She has never said what happened at the vent. She came down three days later with her robe burnt to ribbons, sparks lifting out of her red hair, and the name, which she had taken back. It is not grief, she will tell you. It is a debt, and the mountain is going to be paid in kind.

She pays it out in fire. A flick of her wrist lays a line of embers across someone that keeps burning after she has turned away, and every one of those small fires feeds her. The more of a field is smouldering, the hotter she runs, which she has learned not to enjoy in front of people. When anyone gets close she turns once and a ring of flame throws them back. Nobody has held her since she was sixteen. She has made sure of that.

When she wants to be finished with a thing, she opens the ground under it. Stone comes up, falls back, and settles as a crown of fire around the vent, exactly what she saw at the top of the mountain.

The survivors are grateful. They also look at her, sometimes, the way their parents once looked up at the slope. She has noticed. She has not yet decided who owes whom.

She was small and quick in a city where being small and quick got you exactly one job, and she did that job, running mostly, and lifting, and once memorably swimming, until she was fourteen and a man twice her size explained to her, at some length and with his hand around her arm, the practical limits of being small and quick.

Vex's entire adult life is a response to that conversation.

She learned her blades in a yard behind a rope-works, badly, alone, and the scars on her forearms are from the first two years of getting it wrong. The rope-works gave her the rest: a weighted hook on a braided line that she can sink into a wall or a shoulder at thirty paces and haul herself along. It gives her the only thing she has ever wanted: reach. Nobody who fights her gets to choose the distance. She goes for whoever stands furthest back and feels safest, arrives behind them, cuts once where it counts, and is gone before anyone has found her.

She cuts to open, not to finish. The blood keeps coming after she has gone, and while her marks are fresh no mending takes the way it should. The three-cut finish is the only time she stops managing the distance and closes it: across, back, and across again through the same line. It is the only moment she is where you expect her, which is why it works.

She is funny, loudly and constantly, and it is armour, and everyone knows it is armour including her. The Emberweave recruited her out of a gaol she had already picked the lock on and was staying in mainly because it was raining. She is loyal to about four people, none of whom command anything, and if you are on that list there is no distance she will not cross to reach you.

She weaves absence. Not darkness; darkness is a thing, and can be lit. What she pulls between her fingers is the gap where a thing was supposed to be, and she has found that if you knot enough of those gaps together, the world around them falls in to fill the hole.

She learned it at her mother's table, where a place was laid every night for a man who had gone over the mountains and not come back. Nobody moved the plate. By the time she was nine the empty chair was the most solid thing in the room, and one evening, reaching across it for the bread, she felt it pull back.

In a fight she works fine before she works large. She draws a strand of nothing to a point and slips it into an enemy, and whatever wards they wear come away with a hole through them. She ties a small knot in the air and the people near it lean toward it without meaning to, stumbling into one another, slower than they were. The more she catches in one knot, the more of the pull comes back into her hands for the next.

When she has time, she ties the big one. For a breath everything nearby slides toward a point that was not there a moment ago, grit and arrows and people, and then the point closes. Those it swallowed are put back, hurt, and for a little while afterward they cannot find a single word. The gap took the next thing they were going to say.

That is the part the survivors describe wrongly. They say it got faster because it smelled blood. It did not. The night she left was an ordinary night. A drunk in the crowd reached into the basket to prove something, and she rose and flared her hood and was not there when his hand came down. She was beside him. By the end of that month a knife-grinder had edged both ribbons in steel.

Someone built Tick to wait. It is sure of that much, though the name and the face have worn smooth over the centuries: an old clockmaker, most likely, in a tower above a town, making one last automaton to keep the hours when his own hands no longer could. Strike the bells at dawn. Strike them at dusk. Simple work, and Tick was made faithful.

Then the clockmaker stopped, the way people do. The town thinned and emptied and fell, and still the bells rang dawn and dusk over roofs with no one under them, because no one had told Tick to stop and it did not know how to decide such a thing for itself. Three cities rose and crumbled around that tower. Tick struck the hour through every one of them, to the second.

The tower went in the end, in an earthquake, bells and all. Tick climbed out of the rubble on the evening of the fourth day and stood in the empty square at dusk with its arm raised and nothing to strike.

It walked, after that. The hours had to go somewhere. It strikes people now instead of bells, in quick bright runs of small blows, the way it used to ring the quarters. It is slow to start, but like any old movement it gains as it warms, and a long fight finds Tick moving at a pace nobody built into it. Sometimes it reaches behind its shoulder and turns the key in its own back, which only the clockmaker was ever meant to do, and runs fast for a while, and feels, briefly, that it has done something wrong. When it is surrounded it spins like the great wheel in the tower, arms out, and everything near it rings.

It would like you to know that it does not mind. It was, after all, built to wait.

Its chimney still smokes above his head, and the soot is baked so deep into his skin that he has been no colour but black for forty years.

Everything about him is tempered. Blows skid off him the way a careless hammer skids off hard steel.

The Briar March is a border country, fought over so long that the brambles have grown up through every battlefield and knitted them into one thicket: a hundred miles of thorn with the rusting armour of nine wars still hanging in it. Miregor rules it because nobody else could survive the job.

He is the size of a small house, a boar that learned to stand and wear plate, with a stag's antlers rising above his tusks, grown so twisted they look like the briar itself. His weapon is a drum of studded iron on a haft as thick as a young tree. He has never once retreated.

He is a king in the old sense, the sense that means he goes first. He stampedes through the whole enemy line to reach the farthest of them, and everything near the place he lands goes down. Then he gores, three savage heaves of the tusks that leave long wounds bleeding. But what his enemies remember is how he watches his own side. Whoever among his people is closest to falling, Miregor is standing in front of them, and part of every blow meant for them lands on him. The March has not had a good king in two hundred years. It has had a very stubborn one.

The Maren Lark went down in six fathoms, close enough that you could see her ribs at low tide from the cliff road, and that everyone in the port understood how nearly the crew had made it. Thirty-one hands. The sea gave back twenty-nine over the following fortnight, in the unhurried way it does.

The other two were the captain, who was never found, and the boy who went below to free the fouled anchor chain, who did free it, and did not come back up. What walked out of the surf eleven years later was not the boy and not only the ship. The sea had taken a hull, a chain and a pair of lungs that spent their last minute doing a job properly, and left all three in the salt until they stopped being separate things.

He came back with the water still in him, and uses it without ceremony. He leaves cold standing pools on dry ground, a few inches deep, and nobody who steps into one walks out the same. When men crowd him he lets a wave off his shoulder the way a hull shoulders one, and they go backwards, and come on again slower. And when a whole company presses in, he opens the ground under them to the depth he knows, and the water closes over their feet and holds them, the way a fouled chain once held a boy in the dark.

He does not tire. The sea is still giving him back, a little at a time, and whatever he spends is quietly replaced. He does not speak. There is a sound he makes, low, that anyone who has worked boats knows as the noise a hull makes when it is holding. Somebody once asked whether he was still looking for the captain. He looked at them a long moment, and went back to the water.

They are not undead and not summoned. They are simply pigs that the barrens kept.

A Cindertusk opens by gouting burning breath across whatever stands in front of it, which is less an attack than a way of finding out where everyone is. Then it rears and comes down, and the ground it lands on erupts — a blast of cinder and shock that lifts an entire front rank off their feet and fills the air with enough ash that the second charge arrives unseen.

Herds are worse than individuals by an order nobody expects, because they cook the field between them. Whole companies have been broken without a single Cindertusk closing to horn range, simply by being made to stand in air that had stopped being breathable.
The astronomers of Carrow built armillar:
The astronomers of Carrow built armillaries to model the heavens: brass rings for the orbits, a lamp at the centre for the sun, clockwork to turn it all. The finest was so exact that on the night the observatory lost Umbris, somebody noticed it was keeping better time than the stars. Then its lamp lit itself, and the whole thing rose off its stand and left through the dome.

There are dozens of them now, and nobody at Carrow will say how. A Luminant Orb is a cage of turning golden rings around a fierce knot of blue-white light, trailing a comet's tail of glow and humming the note of its own gears.

It fights like a lens. The light at its heart narrows to a single line and goes straight through the enemy rank to the farthest one standing. When threatened it flares, a burst like sunrise in a shuttered room, and whoever it faces stands blinded for a breath, along with everyone beside them. The astronomers who study the Orbs wear smoked glass. They learned that from the ones who did not.
The banner had an antlered head on it lo:
The banner had an antlered head on it long before he did. It belonged to the Fourth Company of the Marches, who chose the sign because a bull moose will stand in a flooded river and refuse the current. They called the banner Greatbrow. They lost it at the ford at Hask, in a war that has since been renamed twice.

He was watching from the alders, young, not yet the eldest of anything. He had spent that grey morning doing what a young bull does when the herd crosses: standing in the deepest water so the calves have something to lean on. The soldiers came down to the same ford for the same reason and did not make it over. Afterward there was a pole in the shallows, a wet blue cloth wound round it, and on the cloth his own face.

He picked it up because it looked like it belonged to him. That is his whole explanation. Nineteen men were still alive in the reeds, and every one stood up when it moved.

He does not understand flags. He understands what happens around them, which is what happens around the biggest animal at a crossing. When he plants the pole, the people near it stand straighter, strike faster and are harder to knock off their feet. When someone starts a spell at his line, he brings the weighted base down like a hoof through ice, and the word dies in their mouth. When one of his own is held or struck senseless, he is over them before they hit the ground. And when the line must go forward, he lowers the antlers, raises the standard and goes first, and whatever is in front is thrown aside.

Somebody once asked him who the banner was for. He looked round at the people standing behind it, and did not seem to understand the question.
The blade is not a sword and he did not:
The blade is not a sword and he did not pick it up. It came out of him at Ferrow Bridge, in the sixth hour, and the surgeons could not agree whether it had grown or arrived. It is curved like a harvest tool, the colour of the inside of a wound, and still warm when he puts it away.

He was a soldier, and a decent one. The veins came first, out of a bottle handed round a trench before an assault everyone understood was arithmetic rather than strategy. It worked. That is the part people leave out. It worked on every man who drank, and most were dead by noon anyway, and the rest died within the year, badly. There is a word for what they became that Carn will not say in front of anyone who might use it about him.

The bottle made him fast, and unwilling to stop, and it put a price on everything. A blow he fully means costs him something to throw, and he throws it anyway. The more of himself he has spent, the worse he is to stand near; past a certain point the blood he has lost leaves him outward all at once, and knocks flat whoever crowded in to finish him. When a whole line comes at him, he draws the blade across all of them in one long pull, and they go on bleeding after he has moved past.

He held the crossing for six hours. The Emberweave counts it a victory. Carn never has. He keeps a count in his head of how much he has paid out in a fight, because nobody has found the bottom of it. People call the count discipline, and he corrects them. It is a man checking, every few minutes, whether the thing doing the fighting is still him.
The boar clans of the southern hills wer:
The boar clans of the southern hills were farmers once, and most still are. The Ironjaws are the ones who found that raiding paid better and never went back. You can tell them from their cousins at a distance by the cloaks, always red, and by the plate of riveted iron strapped over the snout and jaw.

The iron jaw is earned. A young raider receives it after his first successful raid, and it is riveted, not buckled, so it never comes off. Old Ironjaws eat through a gap between the plates. They consider this a matter of pride.

They fight in the loud, practical style of people who do this for a living. The axe comes round in a wide flat sweep that takes everyone in front of it at once, like a scythe through standing corn. When a fight runs long, he stamps and kicks at the ground in the beat of the clan war drum, and his swings come faster and faster until the axe is a blur. Nobody has ever heard of an Ironjaw raid being called off. They simply end.
The building is still there. That is the:
The building is still there. That is the part people forget when they tell Grimsby as a ghost story. There is a real address on a real street, it is still collecting, and the papers that flutter around him are the actual notices, going back two hundred years, because he has never once thrown a document away.

He was the landlord. Not a cruel one, by the standards of a bad century. He raised rents when rents were raised and slept adequately. When the fever came through the tenements he left, locked the doors behind him, and reasoned that he had no obligation to stay. Ninety-one people were in the building. The ledger recorded them as in grimsby, because they had been, and because that was the only column he had for people.

Whatever came for him afterwards did not kill him and did not exactly punish him. It corrected the ledger. He is now the tenant of record. The debt is his, ninety-one entries compounding for two centuries at a rate he set himself, and he cannot pay it and cannot die and cannot stop collecting, because the only instrument he was ever given for making a thing right is a notice served on somebody else.

So he serves them. A notice pinned to one enemy grows heavier the longer it goes unpaid, and it does not end with the debtor. Anyone who crowds his desk is drawn in close and finds they have nothing to say. Once in a fight he slams the ledger shut, and the whole field is served at once, and bleeds for it.

Nothing settles near him. A wound that should close stays open; a poison that should run its course keeps running. He is not doing it deliberately. He wails because he is aware of this, and has been for a very long time.
The colony had a court because the colon:
The colony had a court because the colony had always had a court, and the court had a magistrate because a court must. When the last queen died and the tunnels emptied and the other ninety thousand went wherever the others went, the court did not rise. Nobody had formally adjourned it. Quorrel, the Magistrant, is very clear on this point, returns to it often, and it is genuinely the whole of his reasoning.

He sat on the bench for eleven days, waiting for someone to say the word. On the twelfth he understood that nobody was going to, and that as long as nobody did, the colony was still technically in session. So he stood, took up all six gavels, and walked out into a world that had never appointed him to anything, carrying the legal tradition of a species that no longer existed. Then, with no malice at all, which is somehow worse, he began to apply it.

He is not a tyrant. A tyrant decides. Quorrel only ever finds, by a procedure older than any living nation. He will hear you, at extraordinary length. What he will not do is let you finish. When a fight grows disorderly he calls the court to order, and everyone within reach is struck and held and cannot get another word out. Interrupt him and you are in contempt: a gavel to the head, and a long moment unable to move. Sentence is passed all at once, down the whole line, six gavels and a storm of paper. He never slows, and he has not slept since the queen died.

The Emberweave uses him and does not look directly at him. Twice someone has floated the idea of adjourning his court properly. Nobody has volunteered to say it to him. He would listen, if they did. He has been waiting to hear it since the eleventh day.
The court is called to order: every enem: The court is called to order: every enemy in the area is struck, held, and forbidden to cast.
The first man Linnet brought back was a:
The first man Linnet brought back was a stranger who fell from a dye-house roof in Carrowell, and she only got him because he had been dead less than five seconds. She did not know then that this was the limit. She knows it now the way a swimmer knows her breath.

She had always seen the threads. Every person is a length of pattern still coming off the loom, the newest rows loose and bright, everything older pulled tight and set. A cut from this morning is already woven in. A cut from a moment ago is only a pulled stitch, and a pulled stitch, she found, can be picked out and done again.

Most of her work is smaller than that. She finds the worst-torn person on the field and runs a line of mending through them that keeps working after she has moved on. She finds the one about to give way and stitches a seam through them so tight that, for a while, nothing will open it. And a gold thread always runs from her to whoever is worst off, so anything done to mend her runs straight down to them. She has not kept a kindness for herself in years.

When a fight has gone badly enough, she takes the shears to it and cuts the last few rows out of everyone on her side and weaves them again as they were a few seconds before, and the ones who fell in that window stand up confused, holding wounds that are no longer there.

Everything older is set. Her mother went into the river at Carrowell eleven years before any of this, and she has sat on that bank more nights than she will admit, pulling at the one thread she can see and cannot reach, as though five seconds were only a habit she might someday break.
The first perfume Velvetplum ever sold w:
The first perfume Velvetplum ever sold was to a coward. He was a young gate-sergeant in the lower city of Sayle, and he came to her shop the night before the siege and asked, in a whisper, whether she had anything that smelled like courage. She was nineteen and newly feathered and very poor. She sold him rosewater for a week's wages and told him to wear it behind the ears.

He held the east gate for two days. When he came back to thank her she wanted badly to confess, and did not, and that night she understood what her trade was. It was not scent. It was the moment a person decides they are more than they were a minute ago.

She has refined it since. Her atomizer finds whoever is flagging worst and mists them, and they straighten and hit harder, and nobody has convinced her it is only the rosemary. Anyone she has made more of grows a little harder to hurt, as if confidence were a coat and she had sewn in a lining. For the enemy she keeps other vials: a slow, sweet note of lily and poppy that drifts across a field, finds whoever is keenest to strike, and puts them to sleep on their feet.

When things go badly she does something she learned at court and never quite approved of. She opens her tail. A hundred eyes unfold in teal and violet and gold, the air goes heavy with every perfume she owns, and her own side comes out of it washed clean and whole while the other side forgets to keep its guard up. It is vanity, deployed. She knows that.

The gate-sergeant is a captain now and still wears rosewater. She has never told him. Some mornings she is no longer sure there is anything else in any of her bottles.
The first thing to understand about Vael:
The first thing to understand about Vaelora Velvetclaw is that she did eat the owl. The people who like her prefer the versions where she didn't. She did. It was the dead of the year on the high moors, she was a thin young snow leopard with three weeks of nothing in her belly, and a great white bird came down onto a fence post in front of her and turned its head all the way round, as if it were curious what she would do. She was not curious. She has never been sorry.

What she had not known was that the owl was the one who carries winter down off the mountains every year, and that winter has to go somewhere. It went into her. By spring feathers were coming in white along her shoulders among the fur, and her breath frosted in midsummer. The moor has had late, strange winters ever since, arriving whenever she does.

She hunts the way cats hunt, which is mostly waiting. She finds somewhere high and goes still, and every moment nobody touches her the strike she is saving grows more exact; the first scratch spoils it, and she sulks. She throws a ring of the owl's flight feathers, frozen hard, through one enemy and into the next. When something swings at her she is simply not in the snow where it swung, and then she is on the weakest thing in the field, because that is what cats do, and she has never pretended otherwise.

When she is done being patient, she shakes out everything the owl gave her, and a blizzard of frozen feathers comes down on all her enemies at once, as silently as owls fly.

Sometimes, on a fence post, she turns her head further than a cat's head should go, to see what someone will do. She knows exactly where she learned it.
The forest does not employ her and she d:
The forest does not employ her and she does not answer to it. She simply noticed, one autumn, that everything that crossed the treeline with a torch came out the other side without one, and decided that whatever was doing that could use a second pair of hands.

She had come into the Tanglewood to die, if she is honest, which she mostly is. She was a charcoal-burner's daughter with a debt and a bow, and she walked in far enough that nobody would follow, and sat down under an oak. Nothing ate her. After three days she got up, hungry and embarrassed, and found the brambles had closed behind her and opened in front, and the path went where she was going before she knew where that was.

She fights the way the wood does, slowly and then all at once. She marks the ground an enemy is walking toward and says nothing, and when they reach it the roots come up around their ankles. Her arrows are blackthorn, and one will go through a breastplate and leave it split like old bark. She does not like to change targets. Given one man and enough time she will find the place he cannot cover, and each arrow lands a little nearer to it than the last. When the whole line comes on she empties the quiver down it, and wherever an arrow lands, something green starts to grow.

The wood has never thanked her, and she prefers that. She still does not know what it wants, only what it will not allow. Some nights she remembers that her father earned his living by the cartload from trees exactly like these, and she keeps her fire very small. She has never been sure whether the forest has forgiven that, or only decided she is useful.
The foundry temples of the Iron Reach ta:
The foundry temples of the Iron Reach taught that metal is purified by fire and people are no different. The acolytes wore red, kept the sacred crucible burning, and once a year poured it over the temple steps to burn away whatever the town had done wrong.

When the ore ran out and the towns emptied, the acolytes stayed, because a crucible is not permitted to go cold. They are still there, in long red robes and spiked iron masks, and whether anything remains under the masks has never been settled; they have not been seen to eat. Some left to tend a larger fire, one that walks.

They have kept the ceremony and extended it to visitors. The acolyte tips its crucible, and a slow sheet of molten flame spills across the ground where the enemy stands thickest and goes on burning there. When anyone comes to object, it draws the heat around itself like a vestment, and most of what strikes it never arrives. They are not being cruel. By their doctrine, they are purifying you.
The glassblowers of Tellary had one hour:
The glassblowers of Tellary had one hour's warning, which is enough to pack a cart and not enough to save a town. The mountain above them had opened in the night, and by morning a river of fire was coming down the valley at a walking pace, and everybody walked. Nobody saw it stop. They came back three days later expecting ash. At the end of the flow, a hundred paces short of the first kiln, stood a shape that had got up out of the lava and was holding the rest back with its body.

He had cooled on the outside by then, into a crust as clear as their best glass, and you could see the fire moving underneath. They called him Pellucid, which is a glassblower's word. The Rook came later, from their board game: the piece that stands at the corner and cannot be moved.

He does not know why he stopped. It troubles him more than anything anyone has done to him since. He only knows he cannot be shifted, not by force and not, the people of Tellary complain, by argument.

He is very simple in a fight. He brings one fist down and whatever is near it stops. He takes hold of the strongest thing on the field and squeezes until the strength goes out of it, the way the mountain once squeezed him. Every blow he takes cools another patch of him into armour. When he means to end it he beats both fists on the ground, again and again, until every enemy for a long way around stands dazed and the light pours through him like a lantern.

The glass never melts back. Each fight leaves him a little clearer and a little colder, and one day, he supposes, nothing will be moving inside at all. He has decided that is a fair price for a town.
The hourglass is not a symbol and it is:
The hourglass is not a symbol and it is not a focus. It is where her heart is, put there by an agreement she made at twenty-six, and the terms are that she will not die while there is sand in the upper chamber, and that the sand is not hers.

She takes it in small amounts, mostly from people who will not miss it, a minute off a sleeper, an hour off a man already spending his badly. She has kept a ledger for a hundred and forty years and can tell you exactly whose afternoon she is standing in. What she cannot tell you is who she made the agreement with. That memory is gone. She suspects it was not taken but spent, by her, on something she judged worth it at the time and can no longer check.

On a battlefield she is a thief and does not pretend otherwise. She finds the fastest thing the enemy has, the duellist whose hands blur, takes the speed out of it and hands it to whoever on her side will use it best. She lets a little of her stored time run into her whole line, so every blow they throw lands with a few more seconds behind it. And every so often she lifts something off one of her own, a poison, a curse, a grief, and puts it in the glass with everything else she carries.

When it matters most, she stops the clock over a patch of ground. Sand bursts out of the empty air, and everyone under it simply is not moving, for exactly as long as she can afford. There is one column in the ledger she has never shown anyone, and it is in her own name.

The Emberweave has offered, more than once, to find her another source. She thanks them, declines, and turns the glass over.
The lamplighters of Sayle had a bad cent:
The lamplighters of Sayle had a bad century. Lamplighters were expensive, and the answer, sold to the council at a very good price, was a street lantern that walked its own route at dusk, lit itself, and walked home at dawn. They worked beautifully for eleven years. Then the workshop that built them closed, and nobody was left who knew how to stop them.

A Clockwork Lantern is an ornate cage of blackened brass around a flame that has not needed oil in a very long time, carried in quick, bird-like hops on jointed brass legs that end in talons. Most still keep to their streets. The ones that have wandered off them are not harmless.

The shutters snap open on one side and the lamp throws a single hard beam across the ground, narrow and white-hot, that scorches everything in its line. Crowded, it opens every vent at once, and the flame roars out in a ring that burns everyone close and throws them back. Somewhere in Sayle there is still a ledger with their routes in it. The lanterns would very much like it back.
The laugh is not a laugh. Everyone gets:
The laugh is not a laugh. Everyone gets this wrong, and Cacklefang stopped correcting them years ago. In her clan on the Chalk Flats the sound means nerves, hunger, a body near the end of what it can stand; the pups make it when they are cold. Outsiders hear it over the grass at night and decide the hyenas find something funny. She has let them.

Her mother gave her the boomerang, a curve of old thighbone, and one rule with it: whatever you throw comes back, and harder. She meant it as a warning about temper. Cacklefang heard it as technique. She throws it through a line of enemies, and the part they never guard against is the return, when it cuts back through the same people with the whole arc behind it.

What changed her was a lean year. The clan followed a herd for nine days and brought nothing down, because she kept picking the strongest animal, the one worth a story. On the tenth morning her youngest sister did not get up. After that she learned to read a field the way her grandmother had: find the one that is limping, the one that has drifted from the others, the one something already has hold of. Point at it. Laugh, so the clan knows where to go. When they close on it, every clean bite gives them breath for the next.

She is not proud of this, and not ashamed of it either. It is how things eat. But when a fight turns and she opens her jaws and lets the whole sound out, one long ragged shriek that tears a wedge through the field and leaves everything in it bleeding, the people watching finally understand. It was never amusement. She has been afraid her whole life. She has simply decided to be afraid at somebody else.
The legions of the old imperial frontier:
The legions of the old imperial frontier were buried where they fell, in the forts they had been ordered to hold, with their pikes beside them and their helmets on. The orders were never countermanded. The empire was too busy falling into the Sundering to send the letter.

So the Bonepike Guards are still on duty: bronze scale over bare bone, horsehair crests gone the colour of dried blood, and the long hooked pike that was the frontier's answer to cavalry. Reach out, catch the rider, bring him down. A Guard uses it now on whoever hangs furthest back. The hook takes them under the arm and hauls them across the field to its feet, and they are held there, helpless, the whole way in.

When the line is pressed it does what it was drilled to do. It stamps and rattles and roars through a jaw with no throat behind it, and every enemy on the field can think of nothing but the skeleton. They hit it, and find it far harder to hurt than it looks. The frontier held for four hundred years. It was never the walls.

The moths of the Emberweave answer to a:
The moths of the Emberweave answer to a queen, and she has lost more of them to fire than to anything else. Most that go into the flame are simply gone. A few, on nights when the fire is large enough and full enough of grief, come out the other side.

A Mourn Moth is one of those. It is the size of a hawk, its wings ash-grey and black and printed with the pale shape of a skull, trailing ribbons of something like burnt cloth. It is drawn to funerals the way its living cousins are drawn to lamps, and the custom of shuttering the windows on the night of a wake comes from them.

In a fight it shakes itself out over the enemy, and grey dust settles over everyone below, and every arm in the cloud grows heavy, every swing a little late, the way mourners move. Then it folds its wings and drops like a stone onto whoever stands farthest away. The moth queen has never called one of them home. Nobody has asked her whether she tried.
The old road from Harrowgate to the sea:
The old road from Harrowgate to the sea makes a long bend for no reason anyone alive can give you. The reason is Oakmir. He was there before the road and before the kingdom that laid it, and for most of that time he was simply an oak: a hundred slow summers, the weight of nesting birds, the year arriving through his roots a month before it arrived anywhere else.

What woke him was a soldier. A skirmish came down the road one autumn and a boy sat against his trunk to die, and did it slowly, and the blood went down to where the roots were. Oakmir drank it. He did not decide to; a root cannot help finding water. But he felt the whole short hurried life going into him, and somewhere in the middle of it he opened his eyes and found that he minded very much, and that there was nothing to do with minding except move.

He has been moving ever since, at a pace that still frightens him. He can set a slow green warmth into one badly hurt friend and let it work through them over the next minutes, or breathe out once and have the whole company feel the ache leave together. When it is very bad he chooses one of them and spring comes up under their feet, the first bloom of the year, early and all at once, and everyone for a long stone's throw around is suddenly half mended and still mending.

He has not forgotten the soldier. In a fight his roots still go looking, and whatever hostile thing stands on them too long is quietly drunk. Left in peace, he only grows. Cut him down and he is up again by morning, a little to the left, a little more stubborn. He has never decided which of those two habits frightens him more.
The ossuary at Harrowmere held the bones:
The ossuary at Harrowmere held the bones of twenty generations, stacked by the monks in patterns: thighbones laid in courses like brickwork, skulls set into the walls like the heads of nails, every name lettered on the lintel above its shelf. It was the most beautiful building in the valley. By the end it was also very full.

Barrowmaw is what the ossuary became when the last monk died and nobody was left to lay the next course. It got up. It is shaped like a great cat or a wolf, depending on how it stands, made entirely of what was on those shelves and bound with the chains that once held the gates shut. Black smoke rises from its mane like grave-damp, and a single violet eye burns in the largest skull.

It hunts names. It breathes a cone of grave air over the enemy that burns the lungs and keeps burning. It hurls its whole weight of bone across the field onto the farthest one standing and scatters everyone around them. And it quickens. At the start of a fight it is slow and deliberate, as the dead are. By the end it is tearing through the ranks like something that has remembered hunger. Every name it takes goes on the lintel.
The rule at the high observatory of Carr:
The rule at the high observatory of Carrow was one candle. A reader could study any patch of the night for as long as a tallow candle took to burn, and no longer. Nobody remembered why. It was written over the door, and the readers obeyed it the way sailors obey a superstition.

Umbris broke it for a gap. Two stars in the southern sky had been drifting apart for three hundred years of records, and he wanted to know why. He lit the candle and watched the dark between them. The candle went out and he did not light another. The others found him at dawn still at the eyepiece, and when they turned him round there was very little of him left to turn. They began sewing a shroud. By the time it was finished there was no body to put in it, only a man-shaped dark that stood up inside the pale cloth and walked out.

He does not so much cast spells as withhold the world. Where the enemy stand thickest he opens a little of that gap, and black mist settles on each and begins to eat. He can mark a single one, and the rot finds them wherever they run. When one dies still carrying it, the rot moves to whoever was nearest, and on to the next. Sometimes he drops the whole gap on a field, and there is a hole in the ground where the light used to be.

He is not cruel. Cruelty needs wanting, and he left most of his between two stars. Someone scratched a line into the observatory wall with a shaking hand: 'It is not that he brings the night. It is that, near him, the day admits it was always afraid.'

The two stars stopped drifting the night he stood up. Nobody at Carrow has looked at them since.
The runesmiths of the old empire did not:
The runesmiths of the old empire did not trust soldiers, so they built their own. A Runic Automaton is a hollow giant of bronze plate hung on a frame of iron bone, and every plate is cut with a word. The words are orders. The blue light burning in its chest is the word at the centre of the sentence, and it is still being obeyed.

Nobody can read the orders now, though scholars have copied whole Automatons plate by plate and argued about the grammar for decades. Its shoulder plates float a hand's breadth clear of the body, held by nothing anyone can see.

It fights by reciting. A single word leaves its hand as a bolt of blue fire and bursts where the enemy stands thickest. When it is attacked it speaks a longer word, and a ring of runes opens on the ground around it, and blows that land inside the ring lose most of their force before they reach the bronze. It is still carrying out its last order. Nobody wants to be there when it finishes.

The thing about Kellsmarch is that nobody agrees on the order. Half the survivors say the star fell and then the lizard walked out of the crater. The other half, the ones who were closer, which is worth noting, say he was already there, standing in the field with his arms out, and that the star came down because he was calling it, and that when it hit he did not burn. Korvux has heard both versions. He prefers the second. He has never confirmed it.

What is not in dispute: he is old in a way that does not match his body, he speaks maybe forty words a week, and he runs hot enough that rain turns to steam a foot above his shoulders. Friends who talk with him come away sunburnt. Enemies who stand near him cook. The axe was not forged. He found it in the crater, or it found him, and it has never needed a fire.

He does not go to the nearest enemy. He goes to the farthest, the one who thought distance was a kind of armour, crossing the field in one burning stride and landing hard enough to stagger everyone near. Then the axe goes round in a single wide stroke, and whatever was in front of him is no longer in the way.

When a fight has gone on long enough, he looks up. A small violet star comes down in front of him, and the crater it leaves goes on burning. People who have seen this tend to stop arguing about Kellsmarch.

He serves the Emberweave on a technicality he considers binding and nobody else understands. Something in the sky owes him. It is paying in pieces, and the pieces come loose more easily in wartime. So he goes where the wars are. He has never said what he will do when it is paid.
The trench where Veyr was born is so dee:
The trench where Veyr was born is so deep that the water there weighs more than stone. Nothing soft survives it. The mantas at the bottom are not the gentle grey fliers of the shallows; they are black, and patient, and they fold the dark around themselves like a coat. One of them folded itself around a drowned child that had sunk from a wreck, and did not let go, and what came up from the trench forty years later was Veyr: a tall blue man with fins where his hair should be and a mantle across his shoulders that breathes on its own.

He calls it his mother when he is being polite and his other half when he is being honest. It moves before he does. When something swings at him the mantle wraps him and the blow meets water, and he comes out of the fold already cutting. Every miss makes him quicker and surer, a little drunk on how little anything up here weighs.

That is the trouble with the surface. After the trench, nothing has any weight. Swords are slow, people are loud and flimsy, and he drifts through fights the way a manta drifts through a current, catching the nearest of them with a hooked cut of his crescent blade and dragging them a step toward him, just to see if they will hold.

They rarely do. So sometimes, when a fight has bored him long enough, he opens a small hole in the air and lets a little of the trench through. Everything nearby slides toward it. Then it closes, all that pressure at once, and when it is over nobody who was inside can make a sound.

It is the only time the world feels heavy enough. He knows that is a terrible thing to want, and he wants it anyway.
The valley of Orrow was abandoned over a:
The valley of Orrow was abandoned over a single summer, after the river changed its course and the fields turned to salt. The people took what they could carry. The cathedral, which could not be carried, was left with its doors shut and its bell-ropes tied, and three days later the last family on the pass road looked back and saw that it was following them.

It has followed ever since, moving the way a building settles, a few yards in a night, with the groan of stone that was never asked to do this, and it rings the hours as it comes whether anyone listens or not. The families who left are long dead, their grandchildren scattered across half the Emberweave, and the cathedral goes after them one town at a time, standing outside the gates like a relative nobody invited.

The first time raiders hit a town while it was there, it did not stand aside. It threw its great doors outward, and the men in front of them went down as if they had walked into a wall. It filled the square with incense so thick the raiders lost the heart to swing, and anyone of its own in that smoke came out clean of whatever had been done to them. Each time its bells rang, the people nearest it felt its stone settle into their skin. And at the worst of it the rose window over the west door caught a light that was not the sun and broke outward, and everything hostile in the square burned in its colours, and everyone else got up.

In Pell, a tanner's widow walks out to it every evening and sits in the back pew, because somebody should. Anyone who stands in its nave is under its protection. Nobody has ever asked for it. The cathedral does not seem to think asking was ever the point.
The windriders of the high passes kept h:
The windriders of the high passes kept hawks, and the hawks kept watch, and nothing crossed the mountains unseen for three hundred years. Then a war that had no use for the passes closed them, and the riders went home, and the hawks stayed. They are still watching. They are no longer sure for whom.

A Zephyr Harrier stands like a man and is built like a hawk: grey-and-white wings, a hooked beak, talons for feet, and a scrap of teal scarf at the throat, the old colours of the pass watch. It carries a sickle, and it comes in on the wind as though the wind had been sent ahead.

It rarely closes to use the sickle. It flicks its wings twice, and two blades of cut air go spinning out at the nearest enemies. If anything reaches it, it beats down once, hard, and a ring of wind and loose feathers bursts out and sends everything close reeling. Shepherds who see a Harrier over the pass bring their flocks down early. It has never taken a sheep. It simply means someone is coming.
There are machines in the deep vaults th:
There are machines in the deep vaults that were never meant to hold a soul, and a period in the last age when several people found out what happens when you put one in anyway. Bitwraith is the residue. Not a ghost — ghosts are continuous. A Bitwraith flickers between frames, present and absent and present again, and the gap is where it does its work.

Its touch is pure static, and it rots from the inside: the wound is nowhere, the pain is everywhere, and healers report the deeply unpleasant experience of mending tissue that is fine and watching the patient continue to fail. When pressed it simply stops being where it was and resumes somewhere worse — always behind, always among the ones who were relying on not being reached.

The vaults are sealed now. This is thought to be a formality. Bitwraiths do not appear to require the machines any more, which raises a question nobody in the Emberweave has been willing to write down.
There is a drowned city off the Hollin s:
There is a drowned city off the Hollin shoals with its gates still shut, and something is still keeping them. Divers describe armoured figures standing at the posts where the city watch once stood, crusted in rose-coloured shell and spurs of coral, each with a spear of branching red coral and a shield cut from one valve of a scallop taller than a man.

Nobody knows whether the Shellguard Sentinels were the watch, or were grown to replace it, or simply moved into the armour after the watch stopped needing it. They do not seem to know either. They know the posts.

Out of the water they do not advance. They hold. The shield comes round in one heavy sweep, and everyone in front of it is knocked flat and left ringing like a struck bell. Then it is planted, the Sentinel sets its weight behind it, and blows that would crack plate slide off the nacre. Divers say the pearl in each shield glows when struck. Several have tried to pry one loose. The Sentinels kept those divers too.
There is a flower at the bottom of the S:
There is a flower at the bottom of the Sunkfen that should not grow there at all. No light reaches it. It feeds on whatever the water brings down: leaves, silt, a drowned sheep, a drowned man. The fen-cutters called it the Sunken Bloom, and for generations it was a story for keeping children away from the deep channels. Then the dykes failed, and the Bloom had more to eat than it had ever had, and it grew.

Nymira is what it became: a tall shape that grew, by accident or imitation, into something like a woman, with a crown of violet petals that open and close as she breathes and a trailing skirt of dark fronds that are not weed. They are tendrils, and they move on their own. Something glows red in her chest, and it pulses when she feeds.

She fights by feeding. Clouds of dark pollen drift from her petals and settle over the enemy, slowing them and poisoning every breath. When they come close, the tendrils lash out together at everyone within reach. And she mends constantly, like a plant turning toward the light; whatever is cut from her grows back. The fen-cutters no longer tell their children about the Bloom. The children can see it from the dyke.

There is a kind of scholar who wants to know a thing, and a kind who cannot bear that a thing is not known, and Meridian was always the second. At nineteen he set out to fill the blank quarter of the Emberweave's oldest chart, the corner where the cartographers had written unsurveyed and moved their pens elsewhere. He came back at fifty-one with the quarter filled, in his own hand, in gold ink, and with the unhurried calm of a man who has seen the last of something.

He does not talk about the thirty-two years. He talks about the map, at length, to anyone, and only later do you notice he has never once said what lives in the blank quarter. Only how far it is, what the ground does there, and which routes will kill you and in what order.

The ink was not his idea. He found it out there, and it took to him the way ink takes to paper: coastlines down one forearm, a mountain range across his back, moving when the world moves. Whatever he charts in it stays charted. When he marks a line of enemies, one small X at a time, their wounds will not close while the marks hold, and some of what runs out of them runs into him.

He fights the way he surveys. Slowly at first, like a man sharpening pencils, then faster by the hour until his hand is a blur. He throws the golden quill through the whole line to the farthest one standing, because the far point is the only one that interests him, and his longest shots land hardest of all. Distance has never felt like protection to him. It feels like an invitation.

He is looking for a second blank quarter. He is fairly sure there is one. He would like very much for there not to be.
There is no story about where the face w:
There is no story about where the face went, because there was never a face, and the people who insist there must have been one are making an assumption about how things get made.

He was commissioned. That much is a matter of record: a contract exists, in a hand nobody has identified, specifying a servant with no name to be recognised by, no face to be described to a magistrate, and no history to be tortured out of an associate. The commissioner died reasonably, of age, in his bed, which is generally taken as the most frightening detail, because it means the thing he built was never once tempted to turn around.

Hollow does not march. When armies form up he is somewhere above, in the part of the sky still dark, waiting for both lines to commit. Then the shadow over their rear rank thickens and lets him out behind the ones with the staves and the scrolls, who thought themselves safest. Whoever there is weakest, he finishes. If they fall, he is gone before the body lands and comes down on the next, and sometimes a third.

Between those moments he works small. A flick of the wrist sends a fan of knives into a crowd, and every cut stays open. He will cut one person three times, and the third cut opens all the others at once. He takes a little back from everything he opens; it is how he mends. Blows aimed at him tend to land in the space he isn't in.

He has no grievance. Everyone wants an origin, some hour in a burning house that would make him legible, and there is only the contract and the work and a preference for doing it cleanly. Twice a commander has tried to thank him. Both times he waited politely until it was over, because it seemed important to them.

There were seven chairs around the table in the back room of the Salt Lantern, and Rafe Marrow sat in one of them with a ship in the harbour and a hand he would have bet his life on. He bet the ship instead, which at the time felt like the careful choice. He lost it to a pair of queens that had not been in the deck when he cut it.

He has spent the years since collecting from everyone who sat at that table. He does not want the ship back. She went down off the Hollin shoals the next winter under someone else's crew. He learned that early and kept collecting anyway, which tells you most of what you need to know about him.

The collecting has a method. The saber is for the ones who argue. The pistols are for the ones who run, both at once, fast enough that the room is full of smoke before anyone has chosen a door. For the ones who run anyway there is the hook, thrown low across the floor, which drags them back to the table and holds them long enough to hear what they owe. He counts his shots out loud, and everyone who has faced him learns that the fourth goes through whatever is in the way: a coat, a breastplate, a closed door. He says four is how many honest cards he was dealt that night.

When he catches one, he pays them back in full, which is his idea of a joke: everything he has in a single blaze, and the lost coins thrown after it, so they go down with their winnings spinning around them.

The list is short now. There is one chair left, the one he was sitting in, and he has not yet decided what the man who put the ship on the table owes.

There were two Corvane daughters and one sky between them, and for four hundred years their family had done exactly one thing: written down where the lights were. The same ledger, in a hand imitated until nobody could tell one grandmother from another. Vesper, the elder, left to be a copyist. Astra stayed and kept the ledger, and thought that was the whole of the inheritance.

Then she found the second book: the same nights and a different sky. A star moved four degrees, a name struck out, a whole minor constellation quietly not there. She spent eleven years on the discrepancy, and somewhere in the eleventh she stopped being entirely a person and started being partly a sky, because if you stare at two versions of the truth long enough you have to pick one to be. She picked the second. Then she learned whose handwriting the corrections were in, and the sisters stopped speaking.

Her skin went the colour of deep water and her hair filled with small hard lights, and she can hold a star the way you would hold a coin. In a fight heat comes off her in every direction, or leaves her as a slow haze that settles on people and keeps burning, and whatever she touches smoulders long after she has moved on.

She has been careful since Vantry, for which nobody has ever blamed her, there being nobody left there to bring the charge. At the end of a fight she does not throw anything. She lets go: she stops holding something together, and the place where she stops folds inward and drags everything near it into one dazed point.

The third book has never been opened. It arrived without a note, in a hand she recognised immediately, and it sits in her orbit unread, and she revisits the decision most nights.
They remember the Long Summer wrong, in:
They remember the Long Summer wrong, in the places that remember it at all: as a golden age, a season that would not end. They did not feel it from the inside, the way the fields did. Growth that could not stop growing. Warmth that thickened into fever. A whole living world beginning, slowly, to rot on the vine because nothing was ever again permitted to rest.

Sylthaine ended it. Not with fire; you do not fight a fever with heat. She climbed to the roof of the world where the last cold still lived, gathered all of it, and pressed it down into the burning heart of the Long Summer, knowing that no living hand could hold that much cold and stay a hand. It cost her the warmth she was made of. It cost her being a woman at all. She lay down over the frozen wound as its final seal and did not move, for longer than anyone kept count. The world got its winters back.

She walks again now, though something beneath a certain glacier does not. She fights patiently, in layers. A sphere of cold sent at the farthest enemy chills everything it passes, each chill makes the next one bite deeper, and she knows to the second when an untended chill will fade. One enemy at a time she stops entirely, locked in clear ice with an expression still on their face. When she calls a storm down she must stand inside it and hold it, the way she once held the seal, and do nothing else until it ends.

She has not trusted a warm thing since, and that includes hands held out to her. She does not speak of what she keeps frozen. Only that it is patient, and that it is warm, and that every year the world she saved grows one degree harder to keep cold.

They still tell it at every fire in the valley. It was cold that morning, mist on the river and frost on the wheat, when the horns sounded off. The enemy came over the ridge in a dark line, a thousand strong and still coming. A boy from the mill dropped his spear and ran, then the man beside him, then all of them. Vael stood there thinking that if he ran too, Ashford would burn. So he did not run. Behind him, Carn and Aureth dragged the gates shut and held the city wall, and the whole town ran them stones and water and anything they could carry. But somebody had to stay out front and thin the horde before it ever reached that wall. He put his sword on his shoulder, walked into the gap where the line had been, and held it.

He roared at the first of them, and something inside him roared louder. The whole first rank broke before a single man reached him. Then he started slashing. One dead, five dead, twenty men slain by his sword. A spear found his side, and he took the spearmen's lives for it. An axe bit into his shoulder, and his next stroke came faster than the last. He should have fallen a dozen times. Something in him would not let him fall. It wanted more. By the hundredth man he was not sated, and the ones still standing feared him bloodied more than they had ever feared him whole.

At the end they closed around him like a fist. He drove his blade into the earth and stood his ground, and nothing they did could put him down.

When the sun went down there were only crows and smoke, and one knight still standing in the field, red to the elbows, breathing slow, and smiling without knowing it. To this day, they call him the Bloodknight.

His armour never washed clean after Ashford; the blood dried into the steel as if it belonged there. His sword is keener now than the day it was forged, as though every life it took left something behind. Some nights, he says, he hears it counting: five hundred and ten, five hundred and eleven, five hundred and twelve. One day he will let it finish.
This is the last chapter. It is the best:
This is the last chapter. It is the best writing in the book, and the Librarian knows it, and that has always been the problem. When he reads it aloud the ink does not step off the page so much as pour, spreading into a pool of black shot with violet light, and something heaves up out of the middle: too many shoulders, too many heads, the shape of a wolf repeated as though the writer could not settle on one.

It was not written to deal with anything in particular. It was written to be what it is. It does not hunt. It turns, every head and claw at once, in a whirl of ink that tears into everything around it, and then it turns again. Blades cut it and the ink closes behind them. It is sturdier than a page has any right to be, because he never once made a thing gentler than it was.

Then the chapter ends, and it goes home. That is the only reason he can read it at all. A town called Brisk once learned exactly how long a chapter is.

Vharok was a warlord, and by the standards of warlords a successful one. He took nine cities of the Iron Reach in a single campaign and lost only one fight, the last, to a fever that bred in his siege camps faster than his surgeons could bury the dead. Dying, he summoned the foundry priests of the last city he had taken and gave them one order: keep me going. They did what foundry priests know how to do. They opened his chest and built a kiln in it.

The air around him is hot enough to burn, and it does, constantly, to anyone who stands near; he does not have to aim it. Cinder Skulks follow him like crows.

Voraxis is a horror of tentacle and toot:
Voraxis is a horror of tentacle and tooth that eats while it fights, and the two activities are not separable. It does not kill a company and then feed. It feeds in order to keep killing, and the fight lasts exactly as long as the food does.

It opens by pounding the earth hard enough to stagger a line, which is a herding move — a staggered formation compresses, and a compressed formation is easier to reach in one movement. Then it hurls its own bulk clear across the field to crash down among the backline, and everything it carves open feeds it, knitting its ruined flesh closed with life that was in someone else a moment earlier.

Killing it is a race against arithmetic. Every hero it wounds is subtracted from your side and added to its, and a company that fights Voraxis carefully and conservatively will lose, slowly, having done everything correctly. The ones that survive are the ones that spend everything in the first minute.

When a star falls, it does not all come:
When a star falls, it does not all come down at once. The heavy part lands, makes a crater, and gets argued about for centuries. The shards fall more slowly, and some of them, over the highest peaks where the air is thin and bitter, never finish falling at all.

Irix is built from those: a roc the size of a watchtower, feathered in blue and violet crystal that rings like struck glass when it moves and throws coloured light across the snow for miles. Nobody knows whether a great bird flew into a shower of falling stars and came out changed, or whether the shards gathered themselves into the shape of whatever owns the sky.

What happens when it comes down is not in dispute. Irix beats its wings once and its outer pinions tear loose and fall like meteors, four at a time, into whoever is nearest. When it chooses a single enemy, it drops out of the sky and takes them in its talons, and for a moment the light goes out over the whole field; when it returns, the victim is lying stunned in the snow. Every wound Irix opens goes on burning with a cold blue fire, like a star that has not finished cooling.

When strangers wade into the sunken halls of Groll, King Bloatus asks their business and waits for an answer, however long it takes. He has sat on the same throne through two hundred floods, and he still believes it is a throne room.

Groll was a green country once, ringed by marsh his people had learned to farm instead of fear. He was not a great king, only a stubborn one, the sort who, told the water is rising, answers that it has always risen and always gone back down. The night the tide took the lower fields, his court begged him to run for the high country. A king who abandons his throne, he told them, is just a large frightened man in a nice coat. Most went anyway, and the fever that rose from the drowned granaries followed them uphill and passed from the dead to the living faster than anyone could dig.

He was still sitting when the water closed over him. The marsh, which he had ruled poorly and loved well, decided it would sooner keep him than drown him. What sat back up wore his crown fused to the bone, and breathed out green.

He did not choose the sickness; it is what he is made of now. When he speaks, his breath hangs over a crowd and will not clear. The reeds that were his subjects hold the ankles of anyone leaving an audience early. When a man dies with the marsh in him, it goes looking for whoever stands closest, the way it did in the camps. Now and then the whole bog heaves and bursts upward in a ring around him, as if the country were clearing its throat.

He was right to stay. Everyone who ran died anyway. He has found no way to be glad of either. He is still waiting for the tide.

When the Tanglewood decides a road has come too far into it, it does not send a ranger. It sends the boars. A Vineback is a wild hog the forest has been growing on for most of its life: ivy through the bristles, moss in the folds of the hide, bramble canes rooted along the spine. Where its hooves strike, green light flickers up out of the soil, and a hoofprint in bare earth has a sprout in it by morning.

It is not clear that the boar minds. It is not clear there is much boar left to mind.

It charges the way boars charge, only more so. Head down, it crosses the whole field for whoever is furthest back, the ones with the torches and the axes, and lands among them hard enough to put them all on the ground. Then it roots, and the earth around its quarry heaves up in a tangle of living vine that locks around ankles and knees and holds everyone in it fast. The woodcutters who worked the Tanglewood roads have mostly found other work. The roads have mostly found other directions.

Where lava meets the sea it cools into black six-sided columns stacked like organ pipes, and on certain stretches of the fire coast the columns get up and walk. The Basalt Mauler is built like a great ape out of those stones: knuckle-walking, arms longer than its legs, a chest that glows faintly through the joints where the rock has never finished cooling.

The iron bands on its forearms are cooper's hoops, and every Mauler wears them. The kind theory is that someone once bound a cracking Mauler to save it, and the rest copied. The other theory is that coopers on the fire coast are rarer than they used to be.

Its fighting is simple. It raises both banded fists and brings them down, and the ground in front of it breaks outward in a wedge that throws the whole front rank off its feet. When it is hurt it hunches and lets the heat rise to the surface, and the outer stone softens, glows, and sets again harder than before. For a while after that, nothing short of a siege hammer does much.

Where lightning strikes a salt flat it fuses the crust into glass, and the flats on the edge of the Bright Waste are strewn with it: twisted tubes and fans and wing-shapes, some the size of a person. The salt-farmers break them up and sell them. They leave alone the ones that sing.

A Saltglass Siren is one of those shapes that kept the note of the storm that made it. It is clear as shallow water, with fins like blown glass and a crest like a spiral shell, and it swims through the air with a low hum that has drawn more than one listener toward it, smiling.

It does not need them closer. It sings its note, and everything in front of it rings and freezes, stunned, the way glass goes still just before it breaks. Then it is gone, the air shimmering where it hung, and it is already behind the weakest thing on the field, striking. The people of the Waste say a mirage only shows you what you are already running toward. The Siren is why they say it.

Wintercrag is a glacier that learned to hate, and the learning is documented — three centuries of survey markers showing an ice field advancing down a valley it had no business entering, against the prevailing thaw, in a straight line toward a town.

It breathes a nova of splintering frost that takes a front rank off its feet, then calls down a howling blizzard that creeps outward across the field and drags everything living to a standstill. Neither is the thing to be afraid of. Every so often the cold simply reaches out — no gesture, no tell, no warning — and stops a heart mid-beat, and a hero standing in reserve at the back of the formation is abruptly a statue that has not yet worked out it should fall.

The town is still there. It pays a levy every year to a company that maintains a line of fire-pits across the valley mouth, and the company's own records make clear that the pits do not stop Wintercrag. They slow it. The levy has been paid, without interruption, for two hundred and eleven years.

Witches were once weighted and thrown off the harbour wall at Low Tessary, on the theory that the sea would take them and keep them. It did take them. The theory broke down on the keeping.

A Kelp Hexer comes up out of the shallows wrapped in the weed that grew over it on the bottom, long black-green ribbons that smell of the tide line. Its face has gone to something bony and fish-like under a crown of coral, and it drifts a hand's breadth above the ground, as if it has not accepted that it is out of the water. In one hand it carries a globe of seawater that holds its shape with no glass around it.

It fights the way it was killed. A bubble of brine closes over one enemy's head and holds them, choking and rooted, for exactly as long as it takes to be terrifying. Then the globe is thrown, cold and hard, and lands with the weight of a wave behind it. Low Tessary stopped throwing witches into the sea a long time ago. It was not a change of heart.
